title: The Fathers on 2 Corinthians
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Paul says God's will, not men, made him an apostle, and he names Timothy as a partner so that their agreement will persuade more forcefully.
comments.comment:
The most wise apostle Paul, appointed to the ministry in Christ, says that he was brought to it by the will of God. … He thrusts aside the reputation of the false prophets and false apostles as ungodly, while he himself speaks in the Spirit and has Jesus dwelling in his own soul, so that he can say in one place, “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 7:40), and in another, “If you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me” (2 Corinthians 13:3). …

By calling himself an apostle of Jesus, he proclaims Jesus to be God by nature and in truth; for no one would be an apostle of men, but rather of Him who is God by nature. He also shows that he was not called to the apostleship against the Father’s will, and that he does not speak from his own heart as the false seers do (Jeremiah 23:16), but serves the oracles of God. … He makes Timothy a partner in the letter, as one who is approved and walks in his footsteps, so that by their agreement he may persuade the more forcefully, since the law says, “On the word of two witnesses and of three every matter shall be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul opens with God's will and why Timothy is named.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul writes to the church of God though the Church is Christ's, and this shows that Christ, born of Mary, is God by nature.
comments.comment: They write to the church of God that is in Corinth, although the Church is said to be Christ’s; for He presented her to Himself as a pure virgin (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:27). If, then, the Church is God’s, and Christ is the one who presented her to Himself, then He who was born of the holy Mary, Mother of God, is God by nature.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul writes to a church that knows him personally, together with his companions, yet he alone is shown to be an apostle of Christ by God's will.
comments.comment:
He addresses all those in Achaia, for Corinth is a part of Achaia. He also addresses the letter as having been written by himself along with Silvanus and Timothy, although he does not always do this; I think he does this when he writes to a church that knows him personally, both himself and those accompanying him in the arrangement.

… nevertheless, even if the letter is from three, he himself alone is shown to be the apostle of Christ through the will of God, not the disciples accompanying him being apostles.

The 'with all the saints' is said ambiguously; for is it 'all the saints with us address you,' or 'we address you with all the saints'? It should not be ignored that in some copies, the present letter is found to be inscribed as being written by Paul and Timothy only.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul does not write alone, and Timothy's part shows the matter is reliable.
comments.comment: Because in the former letter he did not reproach alone, and now in comforting he does not write alone, but by the reception of holy Timothy he shows the matter reliable (2 Cor 1:1–2).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: By naming Christ with the Father as co-giver of grace and peace, Paul shows that he knew the Son to be God by nature.
comments.comment:
If he had known that the Son was not God by nature, how could he not have had to say instead, “Grace to you and peace from God the Father alone”? But as it is, by including Christ with the Father and making Him a co-giver of whatever the divine nature bestows, he plainly shows that he knew full well that the Son is God by nature. …

In naming Christ Jesus, he means the Word from God who appeared in the flesh. And if He gives the very things the Father Himself gives, how is Christ not understood to be God by nature, even in the union with His own flesh that belongs to the plan of salvation? So too the most wise Paul says somewhere of those from Israel, “Theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, comes the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen” (Romans 9:5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul names the Lord Jesus together with God the Father as the giver of grace and peace.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Grace and peace are one gift from Father and Son together, and though believers become sons of God they remain slaves of the Lord Jesus, their Creator.
comments.comment: Those writing pray that grace and peace may exist for the Corinthians from God the Father and Lord Jesus Christ, which is clearly a gift given from Father and Son; for just as the works which the Father does, the Son likewise presents, so just as the gifts which the Father gives, the Son bestows; for one grace and one peace is given toward the Trinity. And this must be said: having said God their Father, they no longer say brother but Lord their Savior, showing that even if the born become sons of God, they remain nothing less than slaves of the Lord Jesus who is their Creator … for he himself, being the Son of God in truth and not by position, is the master of those being made sons.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God alone is blessed in giving blessing without receiving it, and he is Father of mercies in essence, the source of mercy and consolation.
comments.comment: The divine words are such, not to receive blessing but to provide it; for just as He alone is holy and good, sanctifying and making others good, and not becoming those things which He makes others, so He alone is blessed, providing blessing but not receiving it. This blessed God exists as God and as Father of the Lord Jesus, God through the economy [God's plan of salvation], and Father through the Word and being the only-begotten Son. He is Father of mercies in essence, being the source of them; for such a one is not found by the acquisition of virtue like those who become merciful. As the heavenly Father, He is merciful; for the Father of mercies imparts to those who hasten to imitate Him, not to be mercy but to become merciful. Along with these, God is the source of all consolation, sympathy, and grace.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to call God the Father of mercies.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul begins with God's mercies and comfort to give the afflicted good hope, and God makes the comfort no small thing.
comments.comment:
… He begins intimately with those being afflicted from the mercies of God and comfort, showing to them good hopes; for if God is the Father of mercies, he would have comforted those being persecuted and afflicted through him.

Comforting, God does not make the comfort a small thing (2 Cor 1:4). He pre-announces these things, because it was going to call back the one condemned through sin by means of comfort.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul's affliction, borne for the Corinthians' salvation because he preaches Christ, becomes their comfort and urges them to suffer the same.
comments.comment: Our affliction becomes comfort to you; for if the apostles are afflicted, much more the others (2 Cor 1:6). Or he also says this: if even we are being afflicted by men for the sake of your salvation, we suffer this, because we preach Christ to you. If we receive comfort from God through you, so that we may be sufficient for your exhortation, so as to urge you to suffer the same things which even we undergo.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms how Paul's affliction becomes the Corinthians' comfort.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The teachers are afflicted for their hearers' progress and salvation, so that they may endure and be perfected.
comments.comment: The teachers say they are being afflicted for the progress and salvation of those being instructed, so that having endurance they may be made perfect, hoping to receive worthy rewards that will be given to the apostles who contend for the truth and to the hearers of these (2 Cor 1:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul shows the Corinthians the great affliction in Asia, so that they see how he and those with him endured persecution beyond their power.
comments.comment: Since they had a share in the sufferings on which there is consolation, it shows to them the great affliction that existed in Asia from the slanderer and the informer Demetrius (2 Cor 1:7-10); and quite so, since he said they suffer for the sake of their consolation and salvation, so that they might acquire endurance working in the same sufferings, he makes it manifest to them how both he and those with him endured persecution and affliction beyond power, so as to be almost despaired of …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul tells of Asia to encourage endurance, and the sentence of death teaches trust in God, not self.
comments.comment:
Not boasting, he recounts the tribulations that befell him in Asia (2 Cor 1:8), but rather encourages them toward endurance of the sufferings. …

… for we have had the decision of death (2 Cor 1:9), through which we are being disciplined not to trust in ourselves but in the saving God and those who forbid themselves to trust in self.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: God stands by to help us, and trust in him guards the living and raises again those who had cast it off.
comments.comment: God stands helping us, so that we may be bold to remain under his providence through and in him; having slightly withdrawn from his help, he persuaded that it is necessary always to trust in him. For such trust not only guards those living in life, but also brings back those having cast it off, raising them again from the dead.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul's words about rescue from death are not about ordinary death, but about the death that tears the soul away from eternal life.
comments.comment: But it is manifest that these matters are not written concerning common living and death; for he says: 'He who rescued from such a great death, and rescues, and will yet rescue, is the one in whom we have hoped' (2 Cor 1:10). For if these things were being said concerning common death, those saying these things would never not die, becoming outside of it according to time, but rather those confirming these things would have died the common death; for they say concerning death that it tears the soul away from eternal life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul asks prayer not that his attackers flee but that his gifts be useful and many give thanks.
comments.comment: He does not pray for those attacking him to flee as if they were lovers of the body, but so that it may be useful to the gifts given to him, so that through many persons of the now and through many of those coming, the preaching that saves them may be thanked …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Great gifts are given in answer to the prayers of many for one person, so those who prayed should join in thanking the God who gave.
comments.comment: In these matters, he teaches how truly great and divine gifts are given, of many prayers being sent up for one person receiving (2 Cor 1:11). Therefore also he says that he is rousing us toward goodwill and disposition toward him: 'I was rescued from such a great death by God, being joined with you in your prayer on my behalf, so that the grace coming to us, the ones being afflicted, from many persons, might be thanked for by many' (2 Cor 1:11). For if many were co-workers with the prayer toward the gift that has come to pass, it is following that these same should thank the God who provided (2 Corinthians 1:11).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul asks for many prayers and what thanks should follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul's boast, witnessed by his conscience, is that he conducted himself in holiness and sincerity, teaching what comes from the holy writings and not fleshly wisdom, and more so toward the Corinthians.
comments.comment: This boasting, which serves as a witness of our conscience, prepared us to conduct ourselves in holiness and sincerity, not by human instruction, but throughout the whole world, and especially toward you. For the one teaching according to the Gospel does not promise a human instruction, but that which comes from the holy writings … He called the wisdom concerning sensible things 'fleshly,' which the one possessing it does not contain the wisdom of the Spirit, regarding it as folly. It is the custom of the Scripture to call the lessons concerning cosmic and material things 'fleshly'; … Nevertheless, even if we have conducted ourselves in holiness and sincerity in the whole inhabited world, we have nonetheless accomplished this more and more toward you.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul's boast is a conscience witnessing that he preaches rightly in plain words, with God's power working faith.
comments.comment:
This is our boasting: that our conscience testifies to us that we preach rightly (2 Cor 1:12). …

We did not teach you other things, agreeing with you, apart from what we now send, but these things which even as you read, being unadorned: whence also you recognize that our word is as an ordinary man, but the power of God working toward faith (2 Cor 1:13–14).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul writes only what the Corinthians read in the Scriptures, which they know in part and will know fully, and they will be his boast in the day of the Lord.
comments.comment: You have received to read the Gospels and the Law and the Prophets; we write nothing other than what you read (2 Cor 1:13-14). For just as those are God-breathed, which we engrave in the epistles, so are they. Therefore, you also recognize this very thing, having a partial discussion until the end. But we hope with God to find that you come to full knowledge until the end, that is, perfectly and without fail; for having known us in part, and always receiving an increase in the knowledge of the things known and other theorems by that knowledge which surpasses, you will have a perfect vision, just as we write the same things to Moses and the prophets and the evangelists; for the God who came to them as the Word speaks in us, being no other than Christ. And I am confident that with your disposition being thus, that you boast in us; for you yourselves are our boasting in the day of the Lord, in which he will judge those who are made manifest at his judgment seat. And it is possible for the illumination occurring in the souls by the true light to be a day of the Lord Jesus Christ (2 Corinthians 1:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul boasts of his approval in preaching, the Corinthians of believing it, and each is the other's boast.
comments.comment: Paul says boasting of himself in those things in which he was approved by preaching; but the boasting of the Corinthians themselves is in the day of Christ, as if they possessed glory in those things in which they received the preaching. I hope that you will come to know, since even now you have already partially come to know that in the day of the Lord we are your boasting, just as you are ours; for those who have preached in those things in which they were approved are venerable, but those who were zealous in those things in which they believed the preaching.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul decided to come spiritually and not carelessly, since one deciding spiritual matters must never be false.
comments.comment: … the matter of deciding through God to come about is not a light thing. Having decided to come to you, I promised this not out of recklessness or carelessness; for not according to the flesh do I decide, but spiritually. It is proper that one deciding concerning spiritual things should nowhere be false, so that his yes may be yes and his no, no.
comments.selected_reason: States plainly why Paul's travel plans were made with care and why his yes means yes.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Because the Spirit of truth fills the heralds of the gospel, they could not be liars, and Paul answers those who slandered him as contradicting himself.
comments.comment:
No one says “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3), and the Spirit is truth, as it is written (1 John 5:6). Since, then, the heralds of the gospel’s divine decrees have their minds filled with truth, that is, with the Holy Spirit, they could not be thought liars; whatever they say about Christ is entirely right and firmly fixed. Christ Himself will confirm this when He says, “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20).

He says this, then, against those who tried to slander him as contradicting himself, because at one time he preached Jesus as God by nature and at another as a man. Of necessity, then, rounding as it were on their unfairness, he assures them that his word had not been double …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul says his word was not yes and no, meaning he spoke the truth without contradicting himself.
comments.comment: … saying, “Our word to you was not yes and no” (2 Corinthians 1:18). That is, he was not at war with himself or sick with inconsistency, praising a thing at one time and blaming it at another, but he spoke the truth in his preaching. So “God is faithful” (2 Corinthians 1:18), that is, free of falsehood and true.
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly what Paul means by saying his word was not yes and no.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unlike the Greeks, who say both yes and no about their gods, the Son proclaimed by Paul and his companions was not yes and no, and every word spoken about him has proved true.
comments.comment:
The learned men of the Greeks will hold differing opinions about the gods they believe in, saying both yes and no; for truth is not among them, but rather falsehood. That is why they are tossed about by differing opinions. But He who is truly and by nature the Son of God Almighty, how could He become yes and no? …

Necessarily, then, the Son who is from Him by nature, “who was proclaimed among you by us, by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not yes and no” (2 Corinthians 1:19). For every word about Him spoken through the voice of those who spoke for God has proved true.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: If the preaching had yes and no, so would Paul's decision to come, but since the word is true the whole decision is true.
comments.comment: … If, therefore, the proclamation had yes and no, my decision regarding my arrival to you would justly have yes and no; but if the word is true, then the whole decision is true. I believe to God that none of those things which we preached is a lie (2 Cor 1:19). For even the Son of God, our Lord Jesus, did not become a liar (2 Cor 1:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the truth of Paul's preaching bears on his own word about his plans.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: All God's promises have their Yes in Christ, in whom we receive every bounty, and since he is the Truth the No is inadmissible.
comments.comment:
And “as many as are the promises of God,” he says, “in Him is the Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20); that is, in Him we have received from God the Father every bounty and every promise. And this is “in the Yes,” that is, in truth; for these things have come to their fulfillment through Christ. For “death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54), the power of corruption has been overthrown, and weakness too will cease, and dishonor besides (1 Corinthians 15:43), just as the most wise Paul also said in his first letter.

We have also been declared heirs and sharers of the very kingdom of the saints. For He in whom is the Yes will Himself say to us at the divine judgment seat, “Come, you blessed of My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). By nature we are servants; but through Him we have been called from slavery to the dignity of the free, from corruption to incorruption, and we have been set free from serving the devil.

Every promise of God through Christ, then, has the Yes alone; the No, which is denial, is altogether inadmissible, for He Himself is the Truth (John 14:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that every promise of God has its Yes in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the Mediator through whom alone the Father is approached, so every prayer reaches its fulfillment through him, and this is the Amen.
comments.comment: That the word is free of falsehood he confirms further, saying, “Therefore through Him also is the Amen to God, for glory through us” (2 Corinthians 1:20). For since He is the Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), through whom alone the Father can be approached, and in whom is every spiritual gift, surely through Him every prayer will also reach its fulfillment; and this is the Amen. The Son Himself has taught us this, saying to the holy apostles, “In that day you will ask Me nothing. Truly, truly, I say to you, if you ask the Father anything, He will give it to you in My name. Until now you have asked nothing in My name; ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full” (John 16:23–24). Through Him, then, is the Amen to God the Father, for glory through us. For it is our custom to close every prayer in the name of Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Christians end every prayer in Christ's name, which is the Amen.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though the Father is glorified through Christ, who as priest offers our prayers, Christ too is to be worshiped and glorified together with the One who begot him.
comments.comment: … So even if the Father is glorified through Him, and since He has been set forth as “a propitiation through faith” (Romans 3:25), and has also become “a minister of the holy places” (Hebrews 8:2) because of His humanity, offering as a priest the prayer of each of the saints as a spiritual sacrifice (for through Him is our Amen), still He could not be thought to stand outside the duty of being worshiped and glorified together with the One who begot Him, both by us and by the multitude of holy spirits above.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Through Christ we say the amen to God, and God's seal marks us as his own like a shepherd's mark on a flock, while the earnest is a small deposit of the whole.
comments.comment: … Through Christ we send up the amen to God the Father, the confirmation toward Christ we received through God; and through the one having sealed us, He demonstrated our belonging to God and our separation from the evil one (2 Cor 1:20–22). For even shepherds place their own seal upon the flocks, distinguishing them from the strangers. Having said 'earnest', He presented that we have received a small deposit of the knowledge, but the perfection is owed to us; for the earnest is a part of the whole.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the seal and the earnest (pledge) in plain terms.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: God the Father establishes us in Christ by setting a right and unshaken faith in our souls, a faith that needs instruction from above.
comments.comment: “Now He who establishes us with you in Christ,” and so on (2 Corinthians 1:21). God the Father establishes us in Christ by setting a right and unshaken faith in the souls of all, persuading them to hold that He is God by nature and in truth, even if He was seen in our form, He who is above all creation having been born of a woman according to the flesh. Indeed, when Peter confessed the faith and said plainly, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16), our Lord Jesus Christ Himself answered, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but My Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). For since the mystery is exceedingly great, it would rightly need instruction from above, from the Father. So it is God Himself, who has also sealed us and anointed us and given us the pledge of the Spirit, who establishes us in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:21–22).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God establishes us in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God seals and anoints us with the Spirit that is Christ's own and the Father's, and we are sealed into the divine image as Christ is formed in us.
comments.comment:
… For while God is said to seal and anoint us and to have given the pledge of the Spirit, it is again Christ who accomplishes these things in us, not as a servant, nor anointing and sealing us with a Spirit foreign to Him, but with the very Spirit that is His own and the Father’s. For the Holy Spirit is in both, because of the sameness of substance, not divided, but as reaching from the Father through the Son to the creation. …

Through Him and in Him we have been sealed into the divine and spiritual image. For the divine apostle himself, writing to the Galatians, said, “My little children, for whom I am again in the pains of birth until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). And if, by being formed into Christ, we gain the riches of the divine image in ourselves, then He Himself is the image of God the Father and His exact likeness, not as we are, called to likeness by sharing in holiness, but rather by nature and in substance. For He who is God by nature can have nothing unlike Himself in the One who is God by nature and in truth and begotten of His own substance.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though the Savior bids us not to swear, Paul calls God as witness to the intention he held in his heart, which those he loved might doubt.
comments.comment: Knowing what was said by the Savior in the promise concerning the not needing to swear, but having an unsearchable word regarding the yes as being yes, and the no as being thus, he seems to be confirming himself here by swearing. And most rightly; for he announces the intention he had toward the Corinthians, and this exists in thought and heart; and since it was likely that those he loved would waver concerning the genuineness of the love toward them, he calls God as witness of the things said upon his own soul, standing over the things lying in secret. … For he says: 'I am coming to you desiring you, and when I do not do this, I again spare my concern toward you; for you know that having come previously to your city, I spent a whole year and six months staying there, rejoicing in seeing you advancing daily in the benefit according to Christ. For I certainly laid before you the common teaching and the mystical traditions; for I made this clear in the letter before this one, urging you to hold fast to what you received. And since now I am precisely convinced that certain false teachers are deceiving, setting aside the resurrection from the dead and the abiding of the soul, and moreover turning away the knowledge concerning the indifferent, for this reason I refrained now, so that a certain healing through letters might be available to stay with you.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul held back from coming to condemn them, wishing to come not as lord of their faith but as a fellow-worker of their joy, since their faith was still unfruitful.
comments.comment: Because there were many complaints against them, he did not want, having gone, to condemn them (2 Cor 1:23–24). The word is spoken incompletely; for he wants to say that I desired to come to you, but not as one who is lord and teacher of your faith. … To correct those among you who stumble, and those among us who stumble, so that we might become fellow-workers of the joy according to God. … And he says 'joy according to God'; for the apostle would not have joined in with them for a worldly joy. … Having spoken of faith, he presented that they are left without works. Therefore, since they have faith as unfruitful and still incomplete, he says he is a fellow-worker to them.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul stayed away so as not to grieve himself or condemn anyone, and grieving them for their own benefit is a proper thing.
comments.comment:
Because of this I did not come, not so that I might not grieve you but myself, and so that I might not condemn anyone on account of what they are doing (2 Cor 2:1). …

He appears to be feeling sorrow—for he who has not been grieved clearly shows that he did not even take heed when rebuked (2 Corinthians 2:2). For even if I grieve you, I am doing a proper thing; cooperate toward my joy regarding your own benefit.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul wrote instead of coming so that he would find them corrected and glad, and wrote with grief and tears out of love, that joy according to God might take away the grief.
comments.comment:
I wrote this, that sparing you, I did not come, so that at the end of this letter, where it lies, lest having come, God might humble me (2 Corinthians 2:3). And because of this I wrote, so that in gladness I might find you having been corrected, so that you might not grieve. Not looking to my own, but to yours I said this; for I know that if you see me rejoicing, you rejoice, and if you see me grieving, you grieve. I wrote these things so that if you wish for me to come to you, you might beforehand correct the faults.

Showing that he makes the same faults his own, he brought grief and tears, which he has love toward them (2 Corinthians 2:4). Having said, I wrote to you, not that you might simply be grieved, but that the joy according to God might take away the grief.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul wrote through much affliction and many tears, not to subject them to rebukes but to remind and exhort them toward perfect virtue.
comments.comment: He rejoices with the apostle to sympathize with the Corinthians, so that those rejoicing may rejoice together. Because I write these things from a sincere disposition, he says, know that through much affliction and pressure of heart, through many tears, the letter is being dictated. For I did not desire to subject you to such rebukes, but rather proofs concerning the dogmas of truth and reminders, and rather an exhortation toward perfect virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly why Paul wrote with tears and what he meant to do by the letter.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul says the offender grieved them in part too, and does not add Christ, so as not to burden them.
comments.comment: If anyone has grieved even him whom you love, he has not grieved me alone, but in part also you, so that I might not burden you by saying even Christ (2 Cor 2:6). And he fell silent from saying 'and Christ,' so that he might not burden you even by saying it.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul calls the condemnation by the many the reproof, and asks them to obey him in forgiving as they did in condemning.
comments.comment: He says 'reproof' is the condemnation from the many (2 Corinthians 2:6). To forgive him this (2 Kor 2:8). Obey me in condemning, obey me also in recalling him who has been condemned (2 Cor 2:9). Forgive him this, he says; … And because of this he shows that he wants them to think the same things about themselves by a disposition toward them.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul forgave the repentant man in the face of Christ, as one who wishes to imitate and be conformed to him.
comments.comment: This has a dual meaning in the one in the face of Christ (2 Cor 2:10-11). For it is shown either in the face, that is, before and seeing Christ, but also in bearing the face of Christ, having been forgiven, knowing that He Himself, judging that all things for blessedness should be granted, has arrived in life. Therefore, bearing the face—for I desire to imitate Him and to be conformed to Him—I consented to the sin of the one who repented; whence also I am encouraged to be of that opinion.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Satan turns even compassion to his use, and we know his thoughts not to act on them but so as not to be ensnared.
comments.comment: For one must not be ignorant of the wiles of Satan, who, as in former times when fornication was occurring, wished to increase the harm, he was arranging the unfeeling state, so that the one caught in evil would not mourn; but now he has persuaded that there should be compassion toward the one ceasing from evil, so that through this he might also destroy you, the arrogant and the proud, against him. … for it is not the knowing, but the choosing, that makes bad things evil. We know, therefore, the thoughts of Satan, not so that we may act according to them, but so that, not being deceived, we may not be ensnared.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A door of the word is opened by the Lord to those who receive it through divine inspiration, when the listeners are ready to receive the instruction.
comments.comment: But discern what he intends: a great door has been opened to me in the Lord; for perhaps a door of the word is opened by the Lord to those receiving it through divine inspiration, but they do not have a preparation from human art. For God says: 'Enlarge your mouth and I will fill it.' And the wise man has cried out: 'Open your mouth with the word of God,' which means being prepared within by desire and readiness to receive the teaching from God. Perhaps the door of the word is opened when the listeners are ready to receive the instruction.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means for a door of the word to be opened.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul seems grieved with the Troas believers who did not hold Titus, and he left despite an open door, either to admonish them or because he could correct matters later.
comments.comment: He appears to have been grieved toward those in Troas, because they did not do much regarding Titus, nor did they hold him until his arrival, but as if they had become lawless concerning the faith, they departed (2 Cor 2:12-13). Thus, admonishing them as unworthy, he departed even though a door had been opened and no one was closing against the proclamation. Or indeed because of this he departed, as being able easily to correct the things there later upon arrival, as no one being there to hinder.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul's route from Troas to Macedonia came through a vision of a Macedonian man asking for help.
comments.comment: It happened to him that the transition from Troas to Macedonia was through a vision (Acts 16:9). For in the writing of the Acts of the Apostles it is said that truly a Macedonian man was shown to him in Troas by way of revelation, commanding: 'Having crossed into Macedonia, help us.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul finds greater grace in what makes him worthy to triumph through Christ.
comments.comment: This is to the one proclaiming our insults and the circumstances through Christ (2 Cor 2:14). But he confesses a greater grace regarding those things through which he is made worthy to triumph through Christ.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: To be led in triumph is to be made known and glorious through trials endured for Christ, which God allows as they proclaim him, since without trials none wins approval.
comments.comment:
… as they are tested and toil, and they glory in the struggles they endure for Christ. For just as Christ was put on display for our sake when He endured death on the tree and was made perfect through sufferings (Hebrews 2:10), so they too say that they are led in triumph for Him, that is, made known to people everywhere and made glorious through trials, and that they conquer the world by being ready to suffer all things, and very gladly, for the name of Christ. For they are sharers in His sufferings and, as he says, partakers “of the glory that is to be revealed” (1 Peter 5:1).

They say that it is God who leads them in triumph, not as handing them over to suffering, nor as heaping afflictions on them, but because, by His good pleasure, as they proclaim Jesus to people throughout the whole world under heaven, they fall into the trials that come for His sake. For without trials it is impossible to win approval. And the fruit of these trials is that they suffer in Christ, that is, for Christ’s sake, which is glorious and full of good hopes.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be led in triumph.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fragrance of the knowledge of God the Father is Christ, whom the apostles preach, and Paul himself teaches this when he says they preach Christ Jesus as Lord.
comments.comment: What, then, is this fragrance of the knowledge of God the Father, made known to the world through the holy apostles, and in every place, as they themselves say? The inspired Paul himself will teach us again when he says, “For we do not preach ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your servants through Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:5); and again, “For I decided to know nothing among you except Christ Jesus, and Him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles are Christ's fragrance to God because he dwells in them, they proclaim him zealously, and they share his sufferings.
comments.comment: They make our Lord Jesus Christ a sweet fragrance to God the Father. First, they have Him dwelling and abiding in them through the Spirit. Then, as they proclaimed to people everywhere and carried about the message concerning Him, they offered to God their zeal in this work like one of the most fragrant incenses. And in a third way, having been conformed to Him, they have been made perfect through like sufferings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in three plain steps how the apostles are Christ's fragrance to God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ could not be the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father if he were a mere man like us, for one who endured death would not give forth the fragrance of the One who knows no death.
comments.comment: How, then, will He who was born of a woman, who endured the cross and underwent death, even though He came to life again, be the fragrance of the knowledge of God the Father, if, as some suppose, Christ is thought to be a mere man like us, that is, a God-bearing man, and not Himself God by nature, even if the Word from God is understood to have taken up the human in the plan of salvation? For by being like us and nothing more, He will not give forth the fragrance of the nature of God the Father; nor would He who endured death become the fragrance of the One who knows no death.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father because in his own nature he spreads to us the fragrance of the One from whom he is, and he has shown the Father in himself.
comments.comment:
So whether the Word from God is thought of with the flesh, or not so, but by Himself, as before He became like us, He is the fragrance of the knowledge of God the Father, since in His own nature He spreads to us the fragrance of the One from whom He is. And if what I say is true, how could He be something that came into being, counted among those who received their being out of nothing? For such a one could not become the fragrance of the One who is uncreated and who does not exist as something brought into being. For we shall not see what has come into being in what never came into being, nor what never came into being in what has come into being.

Yet the Son has shown the Father in Himself; therefore He is God by nature, because of the sameness of substance. So let the Son hear from us as well, “Your name is ointment poured out” (Song of Songs 1:3); for through Him and in Him we have come to know the God and Father from whom He was begotten.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The same fragrance of Christ leads some from death to death and others from life to life, as a scent or healthy food can help some and harm others.
comments.comment: Because of this, he says, God makes manifest through us the fragrance of the knowledge of Christ in every place, since we are the fragrance of Christ (2 Cor 2:14-16); for just as the partakers, being of His light, are the light of the world, so also, being of the scent, those united to Him are His fragrance. And this fragrant breath is, for some, a scent from death to death, and for others, a scent from life to life. But one must not ask why it becomes a scent from death to death; for it happens to those to whom this occurs as it appears, just as healthy food seems to harm those who offer it at an unseasonable time. For those who, being under death, receive that which comes upon them through sin, do not receive the divine knowledge with right judgment, but come from the death of practical sins to the death that follows ungodly thoughts, just as it carries those receiving it with deeds from life to life. For just as a perceptible scent, being contributed toward health and well-being, harms small animals that do not possess its most acute breath, so the divine fragrance also benefits and leads toward health, and rather toward life, those who observe the image and likeness of God …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who believe receive the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father from life to life, while those who thrust the faith away receive it from death to death.
comments.comment:
But they say that they themselves are the fragrance of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life (2 Corinthians 2:15–16). …

Those being saved and those perishing, then, may fittingly be understood by us, at least according to the aim proper to spiritual contemplation, as those who believe and those who thrust the faith away. Some have not yet known Him who is God by nature and in truth, but have worshiped the creation rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25). These do not accept the message of the divine preaching; they laugh it to scorn instead and think the mystery of Christ foolishness (1 Corinthians 1:23), and so they receive “the fragrance of the knowledge” of the Father (2 Corinthians 2:14) from death to death. For since they are in death through the ignorance and hardness within them, they would all but stumble into a second death as well and be caught by it (Revelation 20:14).

But those who have been brought through the training of the law to the beginnings of the knowledge of God are in a certain sense in life; yet if they should believe, they will receive the fragrance of the knowledge of the Father from life to life. For Christ says somewhere to His Father and God in the heavens, “And this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent” (John 17:3).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be a fragrance from death to death or from life to life.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hard to find is one who can speak the mystery of Christ rightly, as the apostles did, who speak from sincerity unlike those who peddle God's word mixed with deceit.
comments.comment: “And who,” he says, “is sufficient for these things?” (2 Corinthians 2:16). And with good reason. For truly hard to find is the one who has the power to speak the mystery of Christ rightly and without error, as the inspired disciples did, who also set right the perversities of those who think otherwise. It is the custom of these people, and they have spent the greatest zeal on it, to peddle, as it were, the word of God (2 Corinthians 2:17), and they love always to make their account of the faith a mixture of deceit and falsehood; for among them one cannot find the truth unmixed and unadulterated. But the divine teachers of the mysteries, speaking in the Spirit, do and say all things as from sincerity, in the sight of God (2 Corinthians 2:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by peddling the word of God and speaking from sincerity.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The word 'many' has several meanings, and here Paul means he does not peddle God's word through cold speech and foolish explanation but offers it purely and sincerely.
comments.comment: … For this word 'many', I say, being homonymous, signifies more; for it is sometimes said instead of 'certain people', as when the Lord says: 'many will say to me in that day' (Matt 7:22); but also instead of those addressed to a few, as in 'many are called, but few are chosen' (Matt 22:14). The word also indicates all people, as in how through the hearing of the one, the many became sinners, as if through the hearing of the one Adam, the many became sinners (Rom 5:12); for all men are under sin having heard Adam. It also indicates the vulgar, as in the present context: 'let not many teachers be you, brothers'; and it also signifies those who are somehow more numerous, just as 'many are rising up against me, and many are saying to my soul'. In the present expression, we are not as certain people trafficking in the word of God, that is, making it vulgar through cold speech and foolish explanation, but as from sincerity we offer it without guile and purely.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To peddle the word is to mix it with circumcision and Sabbaths or treat piety as profit, whereas Paul speaks sincerely from God.
comments.comment: He says that to peddle the word means to mingle with circumcision and keep Sabbaths, or to think that some consider piety to be a profit. I say, however, that he speaks from sincerity, and says that this very thing is from God, and not from a private power. … He says this because there were also false apostles who considered the word concerning piety to be a profit. …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul needs no recommendation of the Corinthians, who are themselves a letter of Christ written with the Spirit and not with ink.
comments.comment: … Thus what concerns us is manifest, as not recommending you to others, nor others to you; for you yourselves are a letter of Christ, ministered by us, truly written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God (2 Cor 3:2-3). For words are inscribed with ink, but a real and contemplative life is characterized with the Spirit of the living God, as one living according to God by the Spirit having been thus written; for the foolish receive the characters from ink as if they were stone tablets for their souls, but those yielding to agreement with the divine in fleshly hearts, that is, sensible hearts, receive the writing from the living Spirit of God …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul guards the Gentile believers against being led into the observance of Moses, and by 'stony tablets' and 'fleshy hearts' he shows that grace is superior to the law.
comments.comment: From here he wants to show how much the law of grace leaves behind, so that none of those from the circumcision, while hypocritically facing those from the Gentiles, might lead them into the observance of the requirement of Moses and the prophets (2 Cor 3:1). This is your faith and your life, becoming a letter to all and a recognition of our preaching (2 Cor 3:2–3). Because of saying 'stony tablets' and 'fleshy hearts,' he shows the superiority of grace over the law … He also shows how much the grace of the Spirit remains superior to the law and the ministry of the prophets' preaching.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul needs no testimony in words, since the Corinthians' own conduct shows them to be Christ's disciples and their teachers approved, and he keeps them always in memory.
comments.comment: We need no testimony in words. For you, who have been shown to be disciples and believers of Christ and are approved by the deeds themselves, crown us your teachers and have shown us to be approved. Therefore “you are our letter, written on our hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:2), that is, kept always and at every moment in the memory that lies within us; for we always take pride in you, he says.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by calling the Corinthians his letter.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ writes his laws on tablets of the heart that can feel, and whoever has the law within through the Spirit is a letter of Christ known by all.
comments.comment: But our Lord Jesus Christ writes His holy and divine laws for us on fleshly tablets of the heart, that is, on tablets that can feel (2 Corinthians 3:3). That is why He also said through the voice of the prophet Ezekiel, “And I will tear out their heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in My ordinances” (Ezekiel 11:19–20). If anyone, then, does not lean on the shadows given through Moses, and does not have the law written in ink as on tablets of stone, but within, in the mind, through the Spirit, he is a letter of Christ known by all men (2 Corinthians 3:2–3).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's tablets of the heart echo Jeremiah's new covenant, while the law on stone became a figure of the hardness of Israel's hearts.
comments.comment:
He seals the words “Not on tablets of stone, but on fleshly tablets of the heart” with the testimony of the prophet as well. For God said somewhere, he says, through the voice of the prophet, “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they did not continue in My covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord. Putting My laws into their mind, I will also write them on their hearts; for this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 31:31–33).

For of old the inspired Moses received the law, our tutor (Galatians 3:24), on tablets of stone, as it is written (Exodus 31:18). And we say that this became a figure of the hardness of heart of the Jews. For it shows rather that the law could not, so to speak, be received into their minds, and that it had settled into them as into stones, only a little and with difficulty, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul contrasts tablets of stone with tablets of the heart.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul ascribes the dignity of the apostleship to God, who gives it through Christ the mediator to those worthy to receive it.
comments.comment: Paul, knowing it well, ascribes the dignity of the apostleship not to human powers but to God, who is mighty in all things and who holds it out, through Christ the mediator, to those worthy to receive it. That is why he says that all good things come to the saints in Christ; for “every perfect gift is from above,” from “the Father of lights” (James 1:17). Yet He through whom all things are, and in whom all things are, is Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6; Colossians 1:16). He mediates between us and God in the saving economy [God's plan of salvation], yet He works all things from God the Father, since He is His very Wisdom and Power (1 Corinthians 1:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by confidence through Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Our sufficiency is from God, who made us ministers of a new covenant, in which the letter is the type in the law and the spirit is the power of worship in Christ.
comments.comment:
But what is the confidence through Christ toward God? Listen as he goes on to say, “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to reckon anything as coming from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 3:5); for “all wisdom is from the Lord” (Sirach 1:1), as it is written; “but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:5–6).

And what is the letter? The type in the law, the things still carried out as in shadows. And the spirit is the power of the worship in Christ, which shows those who approach it through faith to be spiritual. As far as the type falls short of the truth, so far, I think, do those who serve it come behind those who minister the truth as priests. For Christ sprinkles us with His own blood, and not only for “the purity of the flesh,” as the rites of the law certainly did; rather He cleanses “our conscience from dead works” (Hebrews 9:13–14) and frees us from transgression. Besides this He also grants us the hope of life; for it is true that “whoever believes in the Son has eternal life” (John 3:36). For He has promised also the resurrection of our very bodies, and their return to incorruption and to a life without end.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by the letter and the spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God made the apostles ministers of the new covenant of the Spirit, giving them the conviction to speak, and it has no successor.
comments.comment: Having called us worthy for the ministry of the word, God made us, not possessing from ourselves any thought as if from ourselves according to divine knowledge; for He himself, the one who gave to us to minister the new covenant, provided the conviction for the speaking. And it is a ministry of the Spirit and not of the letter which we were believed to have—for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life (2 Cor 3:6)—the new covenant of the life-giving Spirit, not an old one; for no other teaching comes after it in this life, for it is without successor.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The letter that kills is not a lie, for its death is praiseworthy and ends the evil life, so that those who receive the law are ready for the Spirit's life-giving work.
comments.comment:
The heterodox also use this expression to slander the old covenant, asserting that the former is the writing that kills, while the new is life-giving as being of the life-giving Spirit; therefore they must be rebuked, being very far from the apostolic mind. For even if the letter kills, it brings a praiseworthy death to those being lifted up; for living in ignorance and wickedness before the reception of the legal teaching, after having received it, they die, casting off the evil life they had.

For in this way they will be ready to receive the life-giving work of the Spirit: for instance, he who is in evil lives according to it, but he who turns away from it casts off the life he had according to it, coming through the doing of the good toward the blessed life; for just as evil and good do not coexist, so also the two lives cannot be at once. The letter is certainly not a lie, having imposed an end upon the bad life; for the life-giving work according to the Spirit will immediately approach.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: By letter Paul meant the sense-bound interpretation of the divine writings, and by spirit the interpretation grasped by the mind.
comments.comment: For Scripture is accustomed to call the things grasped by the mind “spirits” and “spiritual,” to set them apart from things perceived by the senses. For example, when Paul says: “But our sufficiency is from God, who also made us sufficient as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:5–6), by “letter” he meant the sense-bound interpretation of the divine writings, and by “spirit” the interpretation grasped by the mind.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The letter is the law, which kills by punishing, and the Spirit is grace, which cleanses and leads to life.
comments.comment: … The letter says the law, but the Spirit says grace (2 Cor 3:6); for the law, while commanding, does not help, but is heavy and kills through punishment those unable to fulfill it, whereas the Spirit makes one clean from sin and provides gifts, clearly leading toward life (2 Cor 3:6).
comments.selected_reason: Says in one plain sentence why the letter kills and the Spirit gives life.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul calls the law a minister of death because it kills those who do not fulfil it, yet he does not slander Moses, and the glory of the law is as nothing beside the surpassing glory of the Spirit.
comments.comment:
And indeed the glory did not come on tablets but on the face of Moses. And wishing to speak here also regarding Moses, he makes Moses evident through the law. He calls the law itself a minister of death, because the law kills those not fulfilling it. And he does not say this as slandering him, for he also said the apostles are a stench of death because of those not obeying the proclamation. …

He calls Moses a minister of condemnation and death—for he condemned in the law those not obeying—and the apostles a minister of the Spirit; for Moses brought down the law, but the apostles conveyed the Spirit to the world. The letter of the law, which was glorified, has not been glorified when examined against the surpassing glory of the Spirit (2 Cor 3:10). …
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul compares the two covenants, both glorified by God but the Spirit's with greater glory, and since the old is abolished with its end in glory, the one that remains has much more.
comments.comment:
… he compares both covenants, the new and the old, each witnessing to the one given in glory from God. However, even if both have been glorified, the one in the Spirit has greater glory. And if, by comparison, the glory of the Spirit is greater, it is not a lie regarding that which it is compared to; for a good thing is more good than a good. …

And it attempts to lead an argument that the ministry of the spirit will be in glory, making the attempt from the lesser; for it says: if the ministry of condemnation had such glory that it could not see all the sons of Israel unto perfection—for it was scarcely veiled—how much more will the spiritual ministry be from glory? Regarding the same view, it makes another attempt, saying: the former scripture, condemning the worthy according to the life of sin which they had, as having brought death as said, is given until a certain time; for this evangelical teaching receives it, being without successor. If therefore that which is being abolished has its end in glory, the remaining, being more, has much more glory; the abolished word is not placed reproachfully.

And certainly the knowledge and prophecy from the part of the saints will be abolished, not utterly, but by the presence of the knowledge of the truth. And just as if we were to say that the introductory teaching is being abolished from the science of the perfect theorems, we do not speak insultingly …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Moses was glorified as minister of the law, but the glory of the proclamation in Christ overcame it and made it seem not to have been glorified at all.
comments.comment: Again he brings the dignity of the divine apostleship back to its incomparable superiority. Having compared the two ministries and set out very well what is proper to each, he shows that the ministry in Christ through the Spirit is the more radiant. This is the aim of his thought in these words, but the saying is not phrased very clearly; for it seems somehow not very easy to see into, nor ready to hand even for those who wish to see it. For what does “What was glorified has not been glorified,” and what follows, mean? What he wants to show is something like this. Moses was indeed glorified, he says, as minister of the law that is being set aside; but the glory of the new proclamation, the proclamation in Christ, overcame the first and made it seem not to have been glorified at all. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains plainly why the glory of the old ministry counts for little beside the new.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As the rising sun makes the moon seem never to have shone, the ministry of the law, though glorified by God, seems unglorified beside the surpassing glory of the gospel.
comments.comment: … [when the sun] rises and spreads out the glory of its brilliance, the light of the moon is overcome by what surpasses it and seems, somehow, never to have shone at all. In the same way, I think, you will take the sense of the words before us. For “what was glorified,” he says, that is, the ministry of the law, though it received its glory from God, seems somehow not to have been glorified at all, because of the surpassing glory, the glory, that is, given to those who serve the divine proclamation of the gospel; for the lesser always somehow gives way to what surpasses it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law's shadow had glory, but what remains in Christ is brighter because it will prevail.
comments.comment: What is being set aside? The shadow and the law, that is, the type. And what remains? The decrees of God. So the shadow too was in glory, but the things of Christ are in a brighter glory; for they remain, since they will prevail over the whole world under heaven.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what is set aside and what remains.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law must cease while the grace of the Spirit remains, and the end of the law comes when the veil is taken away through faith in Christ.
comments.comment: … [Paul] showed that it was necessary to cease and to be idle regarding the law, but the grace of the Spirit, having been opposed to the law, remains. … He says immediately: until today they have a veil. The end of the law is when the veil is taken away and they behold the glory of the Spirit, because in Christ it is made void, that is, it is through the faith into him.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The hope is to be made sufficient by God as ministers of the new covenant, so they speak boldly, and the Spirit makes the faithful understand deep sayings.
comments.comment: What hope? That of being made sufficient by God and fully fitted through grace to be “ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter” (2 Corinthians 3:6). It befits such men to speak with great boldness, ashamed neither of the weakness of the types nor of the lack of learning in their hearers; for the Holy Spirit, settled in the souls of the faithful, makes them understand with ease even the deep sayings.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the hope behind Paul's boldness.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul speaks with boldness as a minister of the new covenant who teaches without a mask, while Moses wore a veil before the many who could not bear the splendor.
comments.comment: Therefore, having such a conviction, being placed as ministers of a new covenant, bringing the teaching unmasked, we use much boldness, being teachers of perfect hearers, since that which we bring to children does not need glory from without, having it by nature. For Moses indeed wore a veil over the face when speaking to the many of the people; for they did not bear the splendor of the teaching. And certainly to the elders and to Joshua the son of Nun, and if anyone was conversing according to them, he was showing the glory naked.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hope is that the grace of the Spirit, unlike the law, remains even after the resurrection, so the apostles teach with boldness and do not imitate Moses' veil.
comments.comment: What kind of hope? That the grace of the Spirit is not made void like the law, but remains even after the resurrection. We, because of the blessed hope of the grace of the Spirit remaining, teach with boldness, and we do not imitate the commands of Moses, who through the veil upon the face signaled that the Jews are not able to gaze intently and realize that the law shall receive an end and shall be idle. The veil remains showing no appearance, that the law is made void upon the coming of Christ.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The apostles' preaching was clear, while Moses, after Israel made the calf, used veils and riddles, teaching through a shadow that has now been set aside.
comments.comment: In this too, again, the disciples of Christ are brighter in glory, because the word of their preaching was clear and not to be withstood, and had nothing hard in it, as the word through Moses did. For since the sons of Israel had proved unworthy, making the calf after so many wonders (Exodus 32:4), Moses put a mask over himself (Exodus 34:33), and in speaking the divine law to them he used veils, teaching through riddles. For they would not have been able to see the true face of the law, that is, Christ, but could barely approach, as it were, a second face, the shadow, which has no glory; and this, the shadow and the type, is being set aside. For it has ceased now that the new covenant has been brought in, and Christ is the end of the law that is being set aside (2 Corinthians 3:13; Romans 10:4).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Moses wore a veil and how the apostles' preaching differs.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the hidden glory of Moses and the end of the law, so when the shadow of the letter is taken away one sees Christ, but the veil remains on those who do not accept faith in him.
comments.comment: So the hidden glory of Moses, Christ, was the end of the law that is being set aside. For if anyone takes away the shadow and strips off, as it were, the outward and second face, the face in the letter, he will see Emmanuel taking shape in many ways in each one, enduring slaughter for the world and saving all under heaven, so that He may be glorified by us and worshiped by the holy angels. So the light of the Savior’s glory is beyond the reach of Jewish minds. For since all spiritual contemplation looks to the mystery of Christ, and the unhappy Jews do not accept faith in Him, the veil has remained upon them, though it is set aside in Christ (2 Corinthians 3:14).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the veil remains for those who do not accept faith in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Moses stands for the law, which hides spiritual meanings under shadows and histories from those who read only the letter and speaks unveiled to those who have ascended beyond.
comments.comment: There are more things symbolically under Moses. For this man carries the face of the law, and since the law is spoken toward intellect and is explicit, it is able to reach only those who approach according to letter and word alone; but covered by shadows and histories, it approaches those who have ascended beyond, delivering the spiritual things according to allegory without a covering. Even if Moses thus conceals certain things, the fault is not his, but of those who are not able to see his glory without a covering, since even Jesus is to be blamed for not making the mysteries manifest to all; for to those outside he spoke in parables (Matt 13:11). So also the evangelical word discourses unhiddenly to those within who have entered into the mystical intellect, making the clarity of the parables, saying to those entering into his house: 'to you it has been given to know the mysteries of the kingdom' (Luke 8:10), but to those outside everything becomes as parables. Certainly, since it is laid out, he shows it; for this reason covering Moses, who has glory upon his face, since the understandings of those not such as to see him nakedly have been blinded. It appears through the whole chain of what is laid out that he calls the law Moses.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The veil still lies on the reading of the Old Covenant because it is abolished in Christ, and those who use the Law as a mirror to see the life in Christ are changed into the same image.
comments.comment: For minds of the Jews that were still rather dull, the outward things of the Law were somehow bearable — I mean again the things through the letter alone — but the things hidden inside were wholly unbearable and not to be approached, and, so to speak, the true face of the meanings. That is why divine Paul also writes to us: 'For until this day the same veil remains on the reading of the Old Covenant, not being unveiled, because it is abolished in Christ. But to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies on their heart.' (2 Corinthians 3:14–15) But let the things of the Jews stand here. 'And we all,' he says, 'with unveiled face, mirroring the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit; and the Lord is the Spirit.' (2 Corinthians 3:18) (2 Corinthians 3:17) For just as those who look in a mirror would gaze at an image and type of the true, and not at the true itself, in the same way, I think, those who desire to see the beauty of the life in Christ would succeed at the thing longed for in the best way by using the Law as a mirror. For remaking the same image of the things into truth, they will know purely what seems most of all good and well-pleasing to God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Moses' veil was taken away when he returned to the Lord, and yours is taken away when you turn to the Spirit.
comments.comment: … Just as Moses, while speaking to the Jews, had the veil, but returning to the Lord it is taken away, and now the Jews, after reading the law and returning the book, carry the veil as if Moses had returned to the Lord. If therefore, having turned away, you come to the Spirit, your veil is taken away just as Moses' was being taken away when returning to the Lord.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: A veil of ignorance lies on the heart of those who read but do not understand what is said figuratively, and it is taken away as God's gift to the one who does all in his power and prays.
comments.comment: Moreover, if the law of Moses had contained nothing written in it to be made known through hidden meanings, the prophet would not have said to God in his prayer: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). But as it is, he knew that a “veil” of ignorance lies upon the heart of those who read but do not understand what is said figuratively (2 Corinthians 3:15). This “veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16) as God’s gift, when he hears the one who has done all that lay in his power, who by practice has trained his senses to distinguish good and evil (Hebrews 5:14), and who says again and again in prayer: “Uncover my eyes, and I shall perceive your wonders out of your law” (Psalm 119:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the veil as ignorance of figurative meaning and how it is removed.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord shows the true face of the law to the wise, and the law leads to Christ as a tutor leads pupils on to something greater than himself.
comments.comment: The Lord Himself is the light, and He “reveals the deep and hidden things” (Daniel 2:22); He shows the true and glorified face of the law to the wise, who are sanctified in the Spirit and made radiant through faith in Christ. For the law leads us like a tutor to Christ (Galatians 3:24); and one appointed to lead others to someone else does not have his pupils stop at himself, but rather carries them on to something better and greater than himself. That is why the inspired Paul says that he counted the things in the law as rubbish “because of the surpassing worth of the knowledge of Christ” (Philippians 3:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the veil is taken away when one turns to the Lord.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We must become spiritual to behold Christ, and then the veil is taken away completely and Moses is seen with his face uncovered.
comments.comment: We must therefore become spiritual, for in no other way is it possible to behold Christ, who is “the end of what is being set aside” (2 Corinthians 3:13), I mean the law. Then “the veil is taken away” (2 Corinthians 3:16) wholly and completely, and they will see holy Moses with his face bare and uncovered, no longer wearing the mask that comes from the letter …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The veil on the heart keeps the sinner from understanding Moses and is the shame of our works, Paul having none, and it is in our power to remove it.
comments.comment:
Much has been said to us about the veil that lies on the face of those who do not turn to the Lord. Because of that veil, when Moses is read, the sinner does not understand him; a veil lies on his heart. Because of that veil, when the old covenant is read, the hearer does not understand. Because of that veil the gospel also is veiled to those who are perishing. So we were saying about the veil that shame is the veil.

As long as we have 'the works of shame,' it is clear that we have the veil, according to what is said somewhere in the forty-third Psalm: 'And the shame of my face covered me.' (Psalm 44:15; LXX 43:15) I have set beside this that the one who has no works of shame has no veil—as Paul was, saying, 'We all, with unveiled face, behold as in a mirror the glory of the Lord.' (2 Corinthians 3:18) Paul has an unveiled face; he does not have works of shame. The one who is not like Paul has a veiled face. …

… So, understanding the veil that lies from works of shame and from such practices, let us take the veil away. It is in our power for the veil to be removed; it belongs to no one else. For when Moses turned to the Lord, the veil was taken away.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever is made worthy of the Spirit is freed from the law's condemnation.
comments.comment: … The one made worthy of the Spirit of the Lord, this one was freed from the condemnation of the law; for through the Spirit the gifts are being worked. And the gift is toward the worthy ones.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Types and shadows cover at times, but the Lord's Spirit, who reveals them, is liberty.
comments.comment: … for it is one thing to be covered at times by types and shadows, and at other times to be revealed without coverings, since we receive its revelation from the Lord's Spirit, being persuaded that the Lord's Spirit is liberty (2 Cor 3:17).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since freedom is wherever the Spirit is, the Spirit is free by nature and above slavery, being the Spirit of the Father reaching out to creation in Christ.
comments.comment: Since our guide into the mysteries says, “just as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18), and, “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17), we will not tolerate the slander of the unholy heretics, who count the Spirit among created things. For if wherever the Spirit is, there freedom surely is as well, how is the Spirit not free by nature? And if that is so, the Spirit stands above the bounds of slavery. For the Spirit is the Spirit of the Father, reaching out from Him to the creation in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unlike Israel, believers behold the Lord with unveiled face and are changed in mind from the law's types into spiritual knowledge, passing from the law's glory to the glory in Christ.
comments.comment:
“And we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, just as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Moses put a veil over himself because the sons of Israel could not look upon “the glory of his face” (2 Corinthians 3:7, 13), for they were unspiritual and fleshly and immature in faith. But we believers, whose heart has been enlightened by the torch the Spirit carries, and whose mind’s eye knows how to see purely, have beheld the Lord with unveiled face. For He has spoken to us and has been seen in glory and in a majesty most worthy of God; for we have known Him as God, the exact imprint of the Father’s being (Hebrews 1:3).

As in a mirror, then, we behold the divine and ineffable nature. For the mind of believers is, as it were, remolded from its schooling in the law into the teaching of the gospel, and is in a certain way transformed into spiritual knowledge. It does not settle for shadow or types, but has chosen to pass from the glory that belongs to the law to another glory, the glory in Christ, through the Spirit. So we are transformed into the same image. For as we carry the types over into truth, and out of the shadow in the law give shape to the mystery of Christ by the fine discernment of our thoughts, we shall find the same glory as if in plain sight. For if glory was given to those who served the law, greater still, and beyond all comparison surpassing the first, is the glory of the holy priestly ministers, who are also made sufficient by God as ministers “of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the unveiled face and the mirror in terms of moving from the law to the gospel.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those moved from the law to the gospel go from glory to glory by the Spirit, who frees them from slavery and also alone reveals the depth beneath the law's spare wording.
comments.comment:
It is plain, surely, and obscure to no one at all, that those who are moved from training in the law to the precision of the gospel would by all means be understood to be going, as it were, from the first glory to another glory, and to be remolded, so to speak, toward better things. And what moves them to this is the Spirit, who sets them free from the slavery that comes from the law; for in the Spirit “we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8:15) as sons and as free.
