There is no other way to see the depth beneath the spare wording of the law except through the Holy Spirit alone; for it is the Spirit who searches “even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). By “the depths of God” we say is meant the knowledge stored up like treasure in the sacred writings. That is why the inspired David made his prayers to God, saying, “Unveil my eyes, and I will perceive Your wonders out of Your law” (Psalm 119:18). And the Savior Himself regarded with no small admiration the one who rises from knowledge of the law to spiritual knowledge, that is, the knowledge of the gospel. For He said, “Therefore I tell you that every scribe who has been made a disciple for the kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who brings out of his treasure things new and old” (Matthew 13:52). The old are the things in the law; the new are the things in Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Another reading: believers, already in glory, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory at the resurrection.
comments.comment: But if someone wishes the transformation of our same image from glory to glory to be understood in another way as well, he will take some such thought to mind: all of us who have known Christ and have been counted among the children of God are by all means in glory; but it is at the time of the resurrection that we are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:18).
comments.selected_reason: Offers a second, plain reading of "from glory to glory".
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Unlike Moses' glory, the glory of God approaches the apostles, who are changed from legal knowledge into spiritual grace and the glory of adoption.
comments.comment:
… We, he says, the apostles, are seen by men with an unveiled face; but having said this, we all demonstrate the common benefit of the Spirit. And for Moses the glory was not approaching the Israelites, but for us the glory of God is approaching; for having established ourselves on faith, we reflect the glory of God, …

We are being transformed from legal knowledge into spiritual grace, moving from the glory of the Spirit working in us toward the glory of adoption. This is made clear by the Lord Spirit, not the Son of God. Just as one sees in that mirror, and another receives the reflection of the one seeing, so it is with the Spirit; for those reflecting the glory of Christ carry a certain likeness from that glory into glory, that is, they receive and take upon themselves the glory of the spiritual image.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Grace gives strength to endure tribulations, while shameful deeds are hidden by those who lack boldness.
comments.comment: He says 'of grace', not 'of the law'; for through the abundance of grace we endure tribulations. The shameful and the base things are hidden, which those practicing strive to hide because of shame; for the base things do not partake of boldness, but wander in darkness.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The gospel is covered only to unbelievers, and the "god of this age" is called God not in truth but by what the nations think, as the belly is called the god of gluttons.
comments.comment:
Even if the gospel is covered, it is covered to the unbelieving, not as the glory of Moses' face was covered from all Israel in the law (2 Cor 4:3).

If the god of this age is said to be associated with reading, it follows that he blinded them. But if God blinded, it was supernaturally, as God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that do not see, and 'I hardened the heart of Pharaoh' (Exodus 10:27) according to the spoken word. Just as it was said of a ruler, not that he is naturally a ruler, but that those deceived showed him to be their ruler by obeying him, so also the god of this age has been forbidden, not as being truly God, but because of what the nations say and think, being called God, just as the belly is called the god of gluttons.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The gospel's light shines like the sun for all, so those who refuse it, like captives who prefer slavery to freedom, have only themselves to blame, and Satan is a "god" only in the thinking of those who do not know the true God.
comments.comment:
“So that the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, should not dawn on them” (2 Corinthians 4:4).

Since the holy preaching shines out like the sun, and every believer with unveiled face beholds “the glory of the Lord” as in a mirror (2 Corinthians 3:18), no one who thinks rightly would lay the ignorance of some to the charge of the divine preaching. For what does it matter if some, though they could know, shake off knowledge, their minds hardened by the devil’s deceit? Those who rise above his perversity, being wise and more discerning, have grown rich in knowledge.

For suppose barbarians had taken some people captive and put them under the yoke of slavery, and someone else offered those who had fallen into this misery release from what had befallen them. Suppose they then preferred to stay under the yoke rather than be free, and so made their misfortune one they could never escape. Tell me, would anyone blame the one who generously offered them leave to go free, or would he not rather charge them with bad judgment?

So the God of all has set before those who are willing to believe in the Son that they may behold His glory with bare and unveiled face. But those who keep the devil’s darkness, which they ought to cast off, and senselessly refuse to admit the light of the gospel’s oracles, have missed the grace. For the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God, would have shone on them as well (2 Corinthians 4:4).

He names Satan “the god of this age” (2 Corinthians 4:4), not because he is God by nature, but because he has been thought to be so by those who do not know who is God by nature and in truth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains who is blinded and why, and in what sense Satan is called 'the god of this age'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the Father's image in essence and by nature, not as we are.
comments.comment: For how else could we understand the light of the gospel of His glory, unless He is understood to be God and the image of the Father, not in the way that we are, but rather in essence and by nature? … He is therefore reckoned as one with His own flesh, and even so He is the image of the Father, in that He is God and has been begotten from Him by nature.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil is called god of this age as the belly is, and every unbeliever belongs to this age, while those worthy of the coming age are enlightened.
comments.comment: He says that the devil is the god of this age (2 Cor 4:4), just as the demons of the Gentiles are gods, and the belly of the gluttons. … the understandings of the unbelievers of this age have been blinded (2 Corinthians 4:4). … For every unbeliever is of this age; for no one surpassing it and being made worthy of the coming age has been blinded in understandings, but has having his eyes enlightened.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A preacher who proclaims Christ and His glory, and not himself, cannot be suspected of deceiving by his word.
comments.comment: It is said: he who seeks his own glory is not true, but he who seeks the glory of the one who sent him, he is true. If we were proclaiming ourselves, it would be suspected that we are deceiving with the word, but if we proclaim Christ and his glory, there is no deception in the preaching.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why preaching Christ and not oneself removes any suspicion of deceit.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul preaches Jesus Christ as Lord and himself as a slave, so it is Christ, not Paul, who lords it over faith.
comments.comment: The present word has a reference to the passage 'not that we lord it over your faith' (2 Corinthians 1:24); for following that, it is said: 'not ourselves we preach, therefore we do not lord it over your faith; for we preach Jesus Christ Lord, and ourselves slaves of you through Christ.' So not we, but He himself lords it over our faith, accepting or judging you according to it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Faith is directed to God even when exercised in the face of Christ, to whom Jews and Greeks alike are called.
comments.comment: By this phrase our guide into the mysteries makes clear that faith is directed to God, even when it is exercised in the face of Christ. For both Jews and Greeks have been called to the knowledge of Christ: the one group, as it were, out of error and false worship into the true knowledge of God; the other, who were schooled under the Law, into a knowledge more exact than that of the Law.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God promised that light would shine out of darkness for us, and the promise is now fulfilled in the dawn of the divine light on the mind.
comments.comment: The mind of those who go astray is filled with a darkness of the mind and with demonic deceit, but God promised that light would shine out of darkness for us (2 Corinthians 4:6). For He said somewhere through the voice of Isaiah, “The people that sits in darkness, see a great light; you who dwell in the land and shadow of death, a light will shine on you” (Isaiah 9:2). And the inspired David says, as if speaking for those in gloom and darkness, “For You will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, You will light up my darkness” (Psalm 18:28). Since the Father’s promise has now been fulfilled in us, and the divine light, seen by the mind, has dawned on us, we have come to know His glory in the face of Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Shows what 'light out of darkness' means, with the prophets' promise.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Father's glory could be seen in Christ only if He is God by nature, and so the Son is the Father's face, image and radiance.
comments.comment: And then, if Christ is not God by nature and in truth, how have we beheld the Father’s glory in Him? Yet I plainly hear God the Father say, “My glory I will not give to another” (Isaiah 42:8); and see, He has given it to the Son. The Son, then, is not other than He, except in His own hypostasis and in His distinct existence; otherwise the Father would seem to have spoken falsely when He set His own glory in the face of the Son. It shows, too, that He who is God by nature is known both in Him and through Him. For the Son is the face and image and radiance of His hypostasis (Hebrews 1:3). The Son is revealed by the Father, and He in turn reveals the Father to us in Himself (Matthew 11:27).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "In the face of" means "through", and the knowledge of God was given by revelation and illumination, not found by reasoning.
comments.comment: In the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6), instead of 'through Jesus Christ', through him. … Instead of 'through Jesus Christ' it shone in our hearts, and the knowledge was not found by reasoning, but was made known through revelation and illumination; for no man could ever reach this, having taken on flesh (2 Cor 4:7–9).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Light shines out of darkness for one who passes from ignorance to the knowledge of truth.
comments.comment: But light shines out of darkness to the one coming from ignorance into the knowledge of truth; … Regarding the darkness named as ignorance and malice which pre-empts men, God shone in the hearts an illumination of practical and intellectual virtue, so that they might have the vision of the glory of Christ in his face.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God hid His treasure in the plain speech of the apostles so that the surpassing power would plainly be His and not theirs, and so that all could understand.
comments.comment:
“In earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7). He calls the plainness of his speech “earthen vessels.” For the divine mysteries were not handed down to us in pompous words, but in the language that everyone is used to, so that all might learn and understand.

What then, Paul? Was it not within the power of God, who makes all wise, to make the holy apostles exceedingly eloquent with ease, far more polished in speech than those others, and skilled at stunning their hearers with the din of words? “Yes,” he says, “for He Himself is the giver of wisdom.” But He has shut up the divine treasure for us in earthen vessels, that is, in a lowly form. For what reason? “So that the surpassing greatness of the power may be of God and not from us” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

For in this way the apostles persuaded all to run to the faith. If their speech had been brilliant, it might at times have seemed that the faith of those who were called was not the work of His power. But since they persuaded with plain words, no one doubts that the surpassing power at work in this came from God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'earthen vessels' as plain speech and why God chose it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Earthen vessels are our bodies, in which the surpassing knowledge of the Trinity is shown to come from God.
comments.comment: By “earthen vessels” we mean the bodies we wear while we live among the things of sense, and we mean it in this way: since, while still clothed in flesh, which hinders the contemplation of the truth, we have the knowledge of the Trinity, the surpassing greatness of this knowledge is made known to us as coming not from ourselves but from the power of God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because the preachers were unlettered laymen, the excess of power in the treasure of the gospel is seen to be from God and not from mortals.
comments.comment: The humble words and the unadorned nature of the interpretation say 'potsherds' vessels (2 Cor 4:7). For if the preachers of the gospel were ambassadors of the truth according to human philosophy, it would have been suspected that men are held by salvation through human art and not from the power of God; but since those ministering are unlettered and laymen, the excess of the power of the treasure according to knowledge will be perceived to be from God and not from mortals. To this is consistent the fact that one is a layman in the word but not in the knowledge, and the fact that 'my word and my preaching are not in persuasions of wisdom's words' (1 Cor 2:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Afflicted names the outward circumstance, distressed the mourning of the will and reasoning.
comments.comment: It is to be known that being distressed is at times the same as being afflicted, and at times something else. For when both are spoken, the being afflicted signifies the external circumstance, the being distressed signifies the mourning in the will and the reasoning. But when both are not taken together, they signify the same thing in parallel.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Though they endured even death for Christ, they still live to God.
comments.comment: For they [the apostles] are seen to have endured even death itself for the sake of their devotion to Him. Yet even if this befell them, still they live, since they are to live to God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God does not let believers be tested beyond their strength, but widens the way for those afflicted for piety.
comments.comment: Through these and the following, he shows that God does not allow to be tested beyond what we are able. For even if we are being afflicted by those who persecute, yet we are not so distressed as to have no escape or recourse anywhere; for God widens the way for those afflicted through piety, as David says: 'In affliction you widened me' (Psalm 4:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Paul's list of afflictions fits God's care for the afflicted.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Humanly the apostles would have despaired, but with God all things are easy and work for their salvation, so they are never lost.
comments.comment: As far as regarding the bitterness of those surrounding us, we would have despaired and we would have been lost (2 Cor 4:8-9); but as far as regarding the God who exhorts, all things are easy for us toward salvation. And even if in every single thing we are being afflicted, being courageous we are not distressed; even if some suppose us as without resource, pursuing and overturning us, but rather we, being resourceful in all things, are not at a loss, we are not lost, we are not cast down; for being overturned by the evil ones we stand unshakeable, being pursued we are courageous, all things being for our salvation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul urged on the athletes by recounting his own sufferings, which reveal that he was handed over to death every day.
comments.comment: Since the difficulty for those contending then was so great, Paul comforted their labor by constantly stirring up the word about the resurrection. And he urges on and anoints the athletes not only by this, but also by recounting his own sufferings. So before he enters into the words about the resurrection, he recounts his own sufferings, saying: “We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed” (2 Corinthians 4:8-9). Through these words he reveals his daily deaths—that they went about like living corpses, handed over to death every day.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead

comments.capsule: Paul's "dying of Jesus" means that, as Christ refashioned human nature in Himself, we too, following Him, have the power of sin made idle in our flesh.
comments.comment:
What, then, is the meaning of their [the righteous ones'] toils? Paul explains it again, saying, “Always carrying about in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in our body” (2 Corinthians 4:10).

We say that the dying meant here is to be understood in two ways: one is inward and spiritual, the other is taken as something felt in the body. For the Only-begotten Word of God, being God and having come forth from God by nature, made His own the flesh that is from the earth, and clothed Himself with this mortal human body, having also a rational soul. And what was the reason for this? That He might put sin to death in the flesh, and blunt the sting of the impulses inborn in it that carry us away to improper pleasures.

It was not for His own sake that the Word, being God, achieved this, that He should be seen above the passions that are in us; for He knows no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21). Rather, He was, as it were, refashioning the whole of human nature in Himself into a holy and blameless life, when He became man and took the form that is ours. For He became “first in all things” (Colossians 1:18), so that we too, following in His steps (1 Peter 2:21), might have His dying in ourselves, that is, the power of sin made idle in the flesh, and so might be able to take up the blamelessness that leads to life.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what carrying the dying of Jesus means for a believer.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A second sense: as Christ died to sin once and lives to God, so those who carry His dying through suffering will live to God a holy and blessed life.
comments.comment:
You may also take the dying and the life of Jesus spoken of here in another way. For He became obedient to God the Father, as it is written, even to death itself (Philippians 2:8), and He laid down His life for the sheep (John 10:11). Yet “He died to sin once for all” (Romans 6:10), that is, for the sin of the world, for He has been set forth as a propitiation through faith (Romans 3:25); “but the life He lives, He lives to God” (Romans 6:10).

This dying, then, which passes through sufferings and reaches even to death itself, the guides into the mysteries carry about in their own bodies, “so that the life of Jesus,” as he himself says, “may be made manifest in our bodies” (2 Corinthians 4:10). For they too will live to God the holy, blameless, and blessed life.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "Always" here does not mean endless but unceasing: those who live in piety struggle for the truth without interruption and are handed over to death.
comments.comment: That which is always and at all times lying before us from the spoken word (2 Cor 4:10-11), does not signify the unending and the anarchic, just as we say the eternal, but the unceasing and the uninterrupted; … But also he will say that one having life and piety and zeal struggles uninterruptedly for the truth; so that we, the living in the said manner, that is, without interruptions, are being handed over unto death.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The apostles risk death as sharers in Christ's sufferings, so that they may share His life.
comments.comment: We always carry the death, always risking because, being partakers of the sufferings of Christ, we are at risk (2 Cor 4:11). The Lord was delivered unto death for us, but we for ourselves through Jesus, so that we might become partakers of his life (2 Corinthians 4:11).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The apostles gladly choose to die for Christ, looking to the rewards to come, and the life of Jesus they will share is incorruption, holiness and glory.
comments.comment:
That he is speaking here specifically of this dying, and of this life, is confirmed for the present by the sense of the preceding verses, which recount the trials and toils that anyone who wishes to complete the glorious course of the apostleship must endure. And he will persuade us no less to think so, all but explaining to his readers what he had said; for he at once adds what follows: “For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake,” and so on (2 Corinthians 4:11).

By these words he shows that they gladly choose to endure the death of the flesh for the sake of their devotion to Christ. For their aim is not to look at present things, but rather to look ahead to what is to come and to the rewards of their toils. They count as nothing the sweat of their struggles and rejoice instead in the good things from above, for they reckon how wide is God’s generosity. This is why they are given over to death for Jesus’ sake, “so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in the mortal flesh” (2 Corinthians 4:11).

And what is the life of Jesus? Incorruption and holiness, and a great glory beyond this world. For so it will be seen by us in its own time, when He comes down to us from above, from heaven, as Judge. And He will “transform the body of our lowliness, to be conformed to the body of His glory, by the working by which He is able even to subject all things to Himself” (Philippians 3:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the life of Jesus' that Paul expects is.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles laid down their lives like their Master, so that others might gain life through faith.
comments.comment: “So death is at work in us, but life in you” (2 Corinthians 4:12). For the guides into the mysteries for the whole world under the sun have imitated their own Master: they too have laid down their lives, so that we who once went astray might gain the life that comes from faith in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in a few words what 'death in us, life in you' means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles risked death so that believers might have life, and they have the same spirit of faith as David, not the spirit of slavery under the law.
comments.comment: Because of the preaching the apostles were risking, but they proclaimed so that the believing ones might live, and this is the life in you (2 Corinthians 4:12). Since, he says, there is a spirit of slavery in the law, but a spirit of adoption in the grace. And he said that we have the same spirit which David also had; the same spirit added the faith, not of the legal slavery. Having, he says, the same spirit as David who spoke according to faith, just as he said: 'I believed, therefore I spoke' (Psalm 116:10).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: "I believed, therefore I spoke" agrees with the heart: one believes in the heart unto righteousness and confesses with the mouth unto salvation.
comments.comment: Regarding this word, [Psalm 116:10] the Apostle says to the Corinthians, 'Having this, we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written: I believed, therefore I spoke; and we also believe, therefore we also speak' (2 Cor 4:13). By saying 'spirit of faith,' he signifies the being which is near from it, the spirit provided by God to the one having faith. 'I believed, therefore I spoke' is in accord with the heart, for it is believed in the heart unto righteousness, but with the mouth it is confessed unto salvation; for he says, 'If you confess the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved' (Rom 10:9).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul says "we do not lose heart", not "do not lose heart", to show that he is in the contest himself, trainer and athlete at once, with the hope of the resurrection.
comments.comment: So when the things brought against them were at their height, then he stirs up the word about the resurrection: “For we believe,” he says, “that He who raised our Lord Jesus Christ will also raise us through Jesus and present us with you. Therefore we do not lose heart” (2 Corinthians 4:14). Having the greatest comfort in their contests: the hope of what is to come. And he did not say to them, “Therefore do not lose heart.” What then? “Therefore we do not lose heart,” showing that he himself was also constantly in the contests. For in the Olympic contests, the athlete contends inside while the trainer sits far off and brings help through words, contributing only as much to the wrestler as shouting and calling out can do. No law permits the trainer to stand near and bring the aid of his hands. But in the contests of piety it is not so: the same person is at once trainer and athlete. Therefore he does not sit outside the wrestling ground, but has thrown himself into the contests themselves and anoints those boxing alongside him, saying, “Therefore we do not lose heart.” And he did not say, “Therefore I do not lose heart,” but “Therefore we do not lose heart,” wanting to raise them up with praises of them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'Therefore we do not lose heart' and the hope behind it.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead

comments.capsule: When the flesh wastes away through suffering or spiritual discipline, the inner self, the mind of the Spirit, is renewed and grows stronger.
comments.comment:
“Therefore we do not lose heart; but though our outer self is wasting away, yet the inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

One may approach the sense of these words aptly by setting the matter out as common, so to speak, to all who have chosen to live in godliness. For “the flesh wars against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other,” as it is written (Galatians 5:17). We say, then, that it is altogether necessary that when the flesh has in some way wasted away and its impulses have grown weak, then above all the other, that is, the mind of the Spirit (Romans 8:6), should grow all the stronger.

The word “Therefore” introduces the giving of a reason, a kind of reminder of something said before. He has said, then: If “we who live are given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus may be made manifest” in our hearts (2 Corinthians 4:11), then, he says, since we hold this hope and rejoice in what is to come, we do not lose heart, for we see ahead of time the beauty of the glory to come; rather, even if affliction comes upon us, we bear it nobly. For even if, being human, we feel pain and suffer some harm in the body, still we are not overcome by these things, for our inner self is being renewed.

This, then, is the sense that applies to all. So when our outer self wastes away through the labors of spiritual discipline, then of necessity our inner self is renewed day by day.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles' bodies were worn down by preaching, but greater labor brings greater repayment of grace.
comments.comment: But you may also take these words in another way. Because they proclaimed Jesus to Jews and Greeks alike, they endured terrible and unbearable persecutions, and their bodies were worn down by the labors this involved. But the greater the labor, the more abundant, I think, would be the repayment of grace that fittingly follows.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul gives a reward before the resurrection: the body, the outer self, wastes away, but in the very affliction the soul, the inner self, grows wiser and stronger.
comments.comment: “But even if our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). See the apostle’s wisdom. He urged them on from what they suffered: “We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed.” He urged them on from the resurrection of Jesus, saying, “He who raised Jesus will also raise us.” Then he stirs up yet another kind of comfort. Since many people are small-souled, weak, and miserable, even if they are persuaded about the resurrection they grow discouraged at the length of time, grow dizzy, and collapse. So Paul gives them another reward and recompense before the resurrection. What is it? “Even if our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.” He calls the body the outer self, and the soul the inner self. What he says is this: even before the resurrection, even before you enjoy the glory to come, you have already received no small reward for your labors from this present time—in the very affliction your soul is renewed, becoming wiser and more reverent, gaining greater endurance, becoming more vigorous and more powerful.
comments.selected_reason: Explains outer and inner self and the reward Paul promises already in this life.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead

comments.capsule: Set against the glory of the coming age, even the heaviest afflictions are light and temporary, and "weight" is a figure from the scales.
comments.comment: If deaths and dangers and temptations follow (2 Cor 4:17–18), how is the affliction lighter? How is it being spent away? For the temptations remained with him and were driving him into old age. How then is the affliction of the saints light? Or is it evident that, being weighed against the glory of the coming age and against the prepared good things for the righteous, even the heaviest temptations appear light to me? And the afflictions are not merely light, but excessive, yet these afflictions fall far short of the greatness of the glory; for the great thing is a body and is heavy. Or he said 'weight' by way of a metaphor of the scales; for the glory, being weighed against the afflictions, is found to be most heavy of all. And he says 'spent away' regarding the temporal; for even if the crushing is long and causes grief, it appears temporal as compared to the infinite glory.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul makes little of the contests and exalts the crowns, calling the afflictions light and the glory weighty, so we should look to the unseen and eternal.
comments.comment:
“For our momentary light affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all measure, while we look not at the things that are seen but at the things that are unseen; for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

He strengthens the resolve of those who wish to compete, making little of the contests while exalting the crowns of the victors, and assigning lightness to the afflictions but weight to the glory. For the assault of the things of this life is measured, because it is temporary, even if it should come “beyond all measure”; yet he says that it will issue in an eternal weight of glory, since the good things of the age to come are beyond words. So we must not look at the things that are seen, which are temporary, but at the things that are unseen, which are eternal.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's contrast of light affliction and weighty glory.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Affliction benefits us even now by making the soul wiser and later brings glory far greater than our labors, since "weight" here means honor, not burden.
comments.comment:
What he means is this: affliction benefits us most of all even here, making our soul wiser and more philosophical, and after this it also procures for us countless good things in the age to come—not merely counterbalancing our labors, but far greater than our wrestling matches, both in quantity and in quality. Paul makes both of these points clear, I say, and he compares the surpassing greatness of the dangers and the prizes, setting the eternal against the momentary, the weight against the light, the glory against the affliction. For affliction, he says, is temporary and light, but the relief—or rather he did not say relief, but glory, which is far greater than relief—is eternal and perpetual and great. By weight here he does not mean what is burdensome and heavy to carry, but what is costly and honored, according to the custom of most people, who are accustomed to call very valuable things very weighty. So when he says weight of glory, he means greatness of glory. Do not think only of this, he says—that you are scourged and driven about—but also of the crowns and the rewards, because those are far greater and more splendid than the present things, and they have no end and no limit.

But these things, he says, are in trial, while those are in hopes; and these are visible, while those do not appear but are suspended and in mid-air. Yet even if they are unseen, they are more visible than the things that are seen. What do I mean, more visible? You can see those things more than these. For these things pass away, but those remain.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead

comments.capsule: Paul calls the things of sense "seen" and temporary and the things of mind "unseen" and eternal, so that longing for them made every affliction seem light.
comments.comment: For to those able to hear he states it plainly, calling the things of sense “what is seen,” and naming the intelligible things, grasped by the mind alone, “what is not seen.” He also knows that the things of sense, the things “seen,” are “temporary,” and that the intelligible things, the things “not seen,” are “eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18). And since he wished to be engaged in contemplating those things, helped by his longing for them he counted every affliction as nothing and as something light. In the very time of “affliction” and toil he was in no way weighed down by them; because of his contemplation of those things he made light of every hardship.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul speaks of two dwellings, the earthly one made by hands and an eternal one in the heavens prepared by God for those worthy to obtain it.
comments.comment: The coming scripture signifies two different dwellings; 2 Cor 5:1 one is earthly and made by hands, … but the other is an unmade dwelling in the heavens, … And he said: 'We have an unmade eternal dwelling in the heavens,' showing that it is from elsewhere, but rather it is greatly prepared for those worthy to obtain it. It is said, moreover, that those things in the promise within it, which eye has not seen, nor any other sense or intellect has grasped, are being prepared by God for those who love him. And the Savior says: 'You have inherited the kingdom prepared for you before the foundation of the world.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some interpreters say that when the thick body, the earthly dwelling, is dissolved, the soul passes to the heavenly dwelling and will receive back what it laid aside.
comments.comment: I have read that the earthly dwelling is called a tent, the body composed of bones and flesh, but the tent being in this dwelling is the form of the inner man, which is a bright and organic body. Those interpreting thus say, therefore: when this dwelling of the thick body is being dissolved, the soul migrates to the heavenly place, called an unmade eternal dwelling. And he shall also receive what he laid aside.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The earthly house of our tent is the body, and when death destroys it the dwelling from heaven, which is incorruption given by God, takes its place at the resurrection.
comments.comment:
“For we know that if the earthly house of our tent is destroyed,” and so on (2 Corinthians 5:1).

By “the earthly house of our tent” he names, in a roundabout way, the tent itself, that is, the body. …

So, he says, we know that when death has destroyed the earthly house of our tent, that is, the body, the dwelling from heaven, that is, incorruption, will take its place before long, at the time of the resurrection, clearly. He says that it is from above, first because the gift is given by God; and then, besides, because all who dwell in the city above, I mean the ranks of the holy angels, are in incorruptible and imperishable bodies, for the nature of angels is free of this earthly grossness. So it is incorruption that he calls “a building from God,” “a house not made with hands,” and “eternal” as well (2 Corinthians 5:1).

“For in this we groan, longing to put on our dwelling from heaven” (2 Corinthians 5:2). That is why we groan, weighed down as we are by corruption, and we long for what is from above …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'tent' and the 'building from God' in plain terms.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The tent is the body, which will be laid aside as corruptible, and God provides in heaven another dwelling, incorruptible and not made by hands.
comments.comment: He says 'dwelling, tent' regarding the body, which, he says, even if it should be corrupted in temptations and dangers through Christ, we shall lay it aside as a corruptible dwelling among the last of things made by hands. But we shall find in the heavens another dwelling, which God provides, incorruptible and not made by hands. … Through the 'putting on', he shows that the corruptible flesh rises up and puts on the immortal; for the 'putting on' is said in reference to another garment. … And he calls the one from heaven 'habitation'—the incorruption from the heavens—since it is not made by hands but is a gift of God.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The soul that has studied wisdom sees that the righteous groan in the tent not to put it off but to be clothed over it, so that what is mortal is swallowed up by life.
comments.comment: Our hope, then, is not the hope of worms, nor does our soul long for the body that has rotted. Even if the soul needs a body for moving from place to place, the soul that has meditated on “wisdom,” according to the words “The mouth of the righteous will meditate on wisdom” (Psalm 37:30), understands the difference between the earthly house that is being dissolved, in which the tent is, and the tent in which the righteous, “those who are” in it, groan, “being burdened,” not wishing to put off the tent but to “be clothed over” it, so that through this being “clothed over” “what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Corinthians 5:1–4).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We long to be clothed with the heavenly dwelling, and the faithful who have put on the Lord Jesus will not be found naked, unlike the unbelieving.
comments.comment:
… For even if the aforementioned tent-dwelling is being destroyed, we are around it, passing from the tent into the heavenly dwelling; but indeed, while we are in it, we groan, desiring to be clothed, longing for the dwelling from heaven, which is this: that we, having laid aside the body, are then enriched from heaven when we have put on incorruption and immortality.

But even if we long for this dwelling, observe whether he who has clothed himself is altogether covered by it; for this is shown by the fact that, even if we have clothed ourselves, we shall not be found naked. Nor is the faithful and holy one found naked when he has clothed himself with the Lord Jesus and the weapons of light and the bowels of compassion before this; for the unbelieving and worthless one, even if he should happen to have the spiritual body which is called a dwelling from heaven, will be found naked, not having striven to have the garments of the inner man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul groans not to be rid of the body but to have incorruption put on over it, and "if indeed" means "when": we shall not be stripped of the body beneath.
comments.comment:
So we groan, not because we desire to be rid of what we now are, but because we pray rather to have incorruption, the dwelling not made with hands, put on over it, “if indeed, having put it on, we shall not be found naked” (2 Corinthians 5:3). For it is true that “a corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom of Solomon 9:15). We have made our being weighed down by corruption the reason for our groaning, and we long to put on over us the dwelling from above and from heaven, that is, incorruption. And what does “to put on over” mean, if not surely to wrap incorruption around the body we now have? So we groan.

“If indeed, having put it on, we shall not be found naked” (2 Corinthians 5:3).

He does not say “if indeed” in doubt, but rather as a declaration, showing it to be firmly settled that when we put on the dwelling from heaven and from above, we shall not be stripped of the tent that lies beneath, that is, the earthly body. So he has put “if indeed” in place of “when,” and the saying means something like this: “When we have put it on, we shall not undergo the laying aside of the first, nor indeed shall we be stripped of the body that lies beneath.” This he makes clear in what follows.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says 'put on over' and 'if indeed'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The question is not only whether we rise but whether, after rising, we will be found naked of glory and confidence before God.
comments.comment: For the question is not only that we rise and put on immortality, but that after rising and putting on immortality, we may not be found naked of glory and of confidence before God—so that we may not be handed over to the fire. That is why he says: “If indeed, having put it on, we will not be found naked” (2 Corinthians 5:3).
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead

comments.capsule: What we want to be clothed with is incorruption, not to strip off the body itself into corruption, so that the mortal may be swallowed up by life.
comments.comment: They are clothed in incorruption. But if anyone is handed over to punishment, he is no different from being naked (2 Corinthians 5:3). The following is intended: that which we want to be clothed with is incorruption, but not to strip off the body itself into corruption. Therefore also it has led to this: so that the mortal might be swallowed up by life (2 Cor 5:5). For this very purpose, it is evident, to become incorruptible (2 Corinthians 5:4).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: We do not want to cast off the tent but to be clothed with immortality, which subdues the tent rather than making it disappear.
comments.comment: Because these things happen in such a way, we who are in the tent groan, being weighed down, especially since the earthly tent has been filled with a very prudent mind. However, even if we are weighed down by having it, we do not desire to cast it off, but to clothe ourselves with the dwelling from heaven, so that the mortal might be held down from below by life; for life does not make our tent disappear when we clothe ourselves with immortality, but rather it subdues it, as the quality of that which we are in mortality becomes more dominant.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul does not want to be stripped of the body but of corruption and death, for the body is God's work and stands between corruption and incorruption.
comments.comment:
The saying seems unclear at first, but it becomes clearer through what follows. For he says, “For while we are in this tent, we groan, being weighed down, because we do not want to be stripped, but to be clothed over” (2 Corinthians 5:4). Do you see how he does not forget himself, and does not call this body a dwelling, but again a tent? “Because we do not want to be stripped, but to be clothed over.” Here he gave a decisive blow to those who slander the nature of the body and accuse our flesh. … What he means is this: We do not want to put off the flesh, he says, but corruption; not the body, but death. The body is one thing, and death is another. The body is one thing, and corruption is another. The body is not corruption, nor is corruption the body. The body is corruptible, but the body is not corruption. The body is mortal, but the body is not death. The body was made by God, but corruption and death were introduced by sin. So I want to strip off what is foreign, he says, not what is my own. And what is foreign is not the body, but corruption. That is why he says, “Because we do not want to be stripped”—that is, of the body—“but to be clothed over” with incorruption for the body. The body stands between corruption and incorruption. It strips off corruption and is clothed over with incorruption. It casts off what it received from sin, and acquires what the grace of God gave. …

So the groaning is not because of the body, but because of the corruption that lies upon it. For the body is heavy, burdensome, and oppressive, not by its own nature, but because of the mortality that was added to it later.
comments.selected_reason: Explains clearly why Paul wants to be clothed over, not stripped of the body.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead

comments.capsule: The mortal is swallowed up by life not by vanishing but by being changed into incorruption, as God renews us through the Spirit to what we were from the beginning.
comments.comment: The mortal is swallowed up by life (2 Corinthians 5:4), not by vanishing or passing into utter non-existence, but rather by being changed into incorruption. For so it was done in the beginning too. It is written that God took dust from the earth and formed man (Genesis 2:7); and so that what is corruptible might be swallowed up by life, for the flesh is corruptible by nature, “He breathed into his face the breath of life, and the man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7). But death came in between through sin (Romans 5:12). Then, as the inspired Paul himself says, the God and Father was pleased “to sum up all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10); for He came to renew us through the Spirit to what we were from the beginning. And it is He who, as God, has prepared us for this very thing and has given us the pledge of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 5:5).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit is the security for coming incorruption, given now as firstfruits and later in full.
comments.comment: So, as a sure security for the incorruption that will be given us in the last times of the age, the life-giving Spirit has been placed in us by Christ: for now, as a firstfruits, but after the return to life from the dead, in full measure.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Spirit's pledge is a gift, and Christ will later add what is lacking.
comments.comment: … [Christ, who gave us the pledge] of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 5:5) as His gift, will at that time add what is still lacking, and “will transform the body of our lowliness, to be conformed to the body of His glory” (Philippians 3:21).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God formed man for incorruption, and the Spirit is the guarantee of it, a part that is trustworthy for the whole.
comments.comment: Then, making the argument about the resurrection more trustworthy, after saying that what is mortal is going to be swallowed up by life, he added: “And the one who worked us for this very thing is God” (2 Corinthians 5:5). What he means is this: from the beginning God formed the human being for this purpose, not so that he might perish, but so that he might journey toward incorruption. … But if someone is weaker and wants to receive another proof and a pledge of the coming resurrection, God gave this too with great abundance, pouring out the grace of the Spirit with great generosity. For this reason Paul, after making the argument about the resurrection trustworthy from the resurrection of Christ and from God being the Creator, adds this saying as well, saying that he also gave us a guarantee—not of money, nor of gold and silver, but a guarantee of the Spirit. And a guarantee is a part of the whole, and it is trustworthy for the whole. For just as in contracts the one who has received the guarantee is confident about the whole from then on and has believed, so you too, having received the guarantee—I mean the gifts of the Spirit—no longer doubt about the good things laid up for you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'pledge of the Spirit' with the picture of a guarantee in a contract.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead

comments.capsule: We hope by faith in the God we cannot now see, and shall see Him as far as a man can.
comments.comment: … while living in the body, that is to say, still passing through this world in the flesh (2 Cor 5:6), we hope through faith toward God (2 Cor 5:7); for his appearance is not visible to us; but this we believe, that we shall depart to him, when we shall see him, insofar as it is possible to see God as a man (2 Cor 5:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'at home in the body, away from the Lord' and walking by faith.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Pleasing God here leads to pleasing Him more there.
comments.comment: If you are pleasing here, you will be even more pleasing there without contradiction, no longer struggling but secure in being pleasing (2 Cor 5:9).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: What can help after death must be gained before it, for each receives what he did through the body, and whether prayers for the dead help depends on the life he led.
comments.comment: This apostolic sentence warns that what can help after death should be done before death, not at the time when each person must already receive what he did before death. But the question is solved this way: by a certain kind of life something is acquired while one lives in this body, so that these things may help the dead somewhat. And so, according to what they did through the body, they are helped by the things that are religiously done for them after the body. For there are some whom these things do not help at all—whether they are done for those whose merits are so evil that they are not worthy to be helped by such things, or for those whose merits are so good that they do not need such helps. Therefore, by the kind of life that each one led through the body, it comes about that whatever is piously done for him after he has left the body helps or does not help.
comments.author: Augustine of Hippo

comments.capsule: Boasting that goes beyond measure is called ecstasy, and the apostles are sometimes compelled to boast so that God may be glorified, though they strive to be prudent.
comments.comment: Those who please men and boast not through piety, it is evident they boast through the face of men; for the heart is observed by God (2 Cor 5:11). Boasting is called ecstasy (2 Cor 5:12). … The boasting regarding the state of affairs is called ecstasy; for boasting has gone out of bounds, while the prudent ones measure. Often, therefore, we are compelled to step out and boast, so that God may be glorified through us. But we strive to be prudent and to measure, so that I may also teach you not to boast.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: "Ecstasy" can mean not only going astray but being struck with amazement at a wonder, so Paul's being beside himself is a divine ecstasy, not a madness.
comments.comment: Let those be reproved by you on these matters—he speaks concerning the false apostles (2 Cor 5:12)—but we do these things for your sake and through you; for even if, becoming outside of men, we stand outside to God, nevertheless we act with prudence toward you, having a divine ecstasy, not a madness (2 Cor 5:13). … But the foolish were deceived by the similarity of names; for the voice that has gone into ecstasy signifies not only to err and to stumble, but also to be struck with amazement at a wonder.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul means by being 'beside himself'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some Jews thought Paul had lost his mind, so he wrote that if we are beside ourselves, it is for God.
comments.comment: For some of the Jews thought that the inspired Paul had, as it were, lost his mind and was setting himself against the laws given through Moses. That is why he writes to those who had believed, “For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you” (2 Corinthians 5:13).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul's being beside himself means standing outside human limits, not madness.
comments.comment: If indeed Paul says: 'whether we have gone out of our minds, it is to God' (2 Corinthians 5:13), he is not speaking of madness, but of standing outside of human limits …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul's ecstasy is explained by the love of God that constrains him: since one died for all, all died, and we now live by the one who died and rose for us.
comments.comment: The type of ecstasy which he undergoes is explained, saying: we are constrained by the much love having come to us of God (2 Cor 5:14), … that if one Christ died for all, then all died; for he would not have died for all, unless all of us were responsible for death. … Therefore, if for our sake and through us he died and rose, having risen with him we live, not for themselves, that is, humanly, but by the one having suffered and risen for our sake.
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'one died for all, therefore all died' and living for Him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: All have died to the world through baptism and life, and no longer live for themselves but for Christ, who died for all and made the world his debtor.
comments.comment:
Desiring to be silent, we are compelled to boast, being compelled by the love of Christ, so that he might be glorified (2 Cor 5:14–15).

All have died; he speaks of the faithful as being dying to the world both through baptism and through life. And they no longer live for themselves; for even I, if I were living for myself, I would not have boasted, but since I live for Christ, through him I am silent if it would be for your benefit, and through him I boast, so that he might be glorified. Whether we are beside ourselves or we act with prudence for you, we do everything through the love of Christ (2 Corinthians 5:13-14). Since he who dies for some rescues those already judged from death, and insofar as we were dead regarding what concerns us, if one died for all, therefore all have died insofar as to the condemnation. But he speaks of the faithful, who through baptism were crucified to the world, no longer living for themselves but for Christ; for Christ, having died for all and having paid the common debt, made the world his debtor.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Each of us owes his life to Christ, who acquired us for the Father by laying down His blood as the price.
comments.comment: Each of us owes his own life to Christ. For as the inspired Paul said, ‘We were bought with a price, and we are not our own’ (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). And, ‘One died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for them and was raised’ (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). For he acquired us through himself for God the Father, laying down his own blood as a kind of price on our behalf.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 16

comments.capsule: We no longer know Christ according to the flesh and the law, but as the God-Word who tabernacled among us.
comments.comment: Since we live by the one having died and risen for our sake, from when we began to be thus, we no longer know anyone according to the flesh (2 Cor 5:16), having surpassed the flesh and its sufferings, and even the shadowy teaching of the law. Even if we had known Christ according to the flesh, still wanting to Judaize and fall to the flesh through the exposition of the law, but now we no longer know him thus, but as the God-Word; for the Word having become flesh, he did not dwell, but tabernacled among us (John 1:14), so that after this we might behold his glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth. For to dwell differs from to tabernacle, just as a house differs from a tent; for the house always remains immovably established, but the tent is a portable dwelling. Certainly those making progress tabernacle, but those having reached perfection dwell; for I shall travel in a place of wondrous tabernacling until the house of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who have the pledge of the Spirit already live as spiritual people, for by "flesh" Paul here means the corruption of the flesh, which we have shaken off.
comments.comment: Those who have the pledge of the Spirit and are rich in the hope of the resurrection lay hold of what they expect to come as though it were already present, and say: “So from now on we know no one according to the flesh” (2 Corinthians 5:16); for we are all spiritual, and not in fleshly corruption. For here, I think, he calls the corruption of the flesh “flesh.” Since the Only-begotten has shone upon us, we have been transformed toward the Word who gives life to all things. For just as we were subject to the bonds of death while sin reigned, so, now that the righteousness in Christ has come in, we have shaken off corruption. So no one, then, is in the flesh, that is, in fleshly weakness. And with regard to the others as well, corruption may fittingly be understood by it.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ, who died in the flesh for all and now lives with the Father, is understood to be above the flesh, and so we, following Him, are to be above the flesh too.
comments.comment: … and He [the Word] underwent death in the flesh for the life of all, and so we have known Him; but from now on we know Him so no longer. For even though He is in the flesh, since He came back to life on the third day and is with the Father in heaven, yet He is understood to be above the flesh. For having died once, He “dies no more; death no longer has dominion over Him. For the death He died, He died to sin once for all; but the life He lives, He lives to God” (Romans 6:9–10). If, then, the Author of our life (Acts 3:15) has come to be in this state, it is altogether necessary that we too, following in His footsteps (1 Peter 2:21), be understood to be not in the flesh but rather above the flesh.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Knowing no one according to the flesh means no longer living by circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath, for Christ, who as a man fulfilled the law, abolished it by dying and rising.
comments.comment: Thus we from now on know no one according to the flesh (2 Cor 5:16). Since circumcision is of the flesh, and this to eat and that not to eat, and the Sabbath, he says that we of the faithful know no one according to the flesh. … for even if Christ was circumcised and became subject to the observances of the law—that is, even if we knew Christ according to the flesh—but now we no longer know him. … For when he was among men, as a man he lived out his citizenship fulfilling the law by his life; but having died and having risen, incorruptible, he abolished the things of the law and showed the way of the heavenly citizenship.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: After the resurrection Paul no longer knows Christ by the measures of the flesh but confesses Him as God, though he knows Him risen in the flesh.
comments.comment: “And if we have known Christ according to flesh, yet now we no longer know him.” (2 Corinthians 5:16) What then does Paul say? Does he deny Christ after the resurrection? Does he not know him raised in flesh and taken up with it into heaven? And who would dare to say that? For thus he also knows him taken up and going to come at the times in the way he has gone up into heaven. How then does he say he does not know Christ according to flesh? Because after the return to life from the dead, it is better to know and confess him not still from the flesh’s measures, but as from divine superiority. For while the economy was not yet fulfilled he was preached according to flesh, so that the Only-begotten might be believed to have become human; but since the mystery has been completed, it is better to confess him from what he is as God than from the having-been-emptied through the flesh. So there is one Christ and Son and Lord.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the puzzle of 'we no longer know Christ according to the flesh'.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: One who shares in Christ is a new creation, as the psalmist asked for a clean heart to be created in him.
comments.comment: He who is in Christ, becoming a participant in him, is a new creation (2 Cor 5:17). The holy one, wishing such a thing to exist in his own heart, said: Create in me, O God, a clean heart (Psalm 51:10). According to this meaning, the Savior creates in him the two into one new man (Ephesians 2:15).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those baptized die to bodily ways of life and become a new creation living by the Spirit's grace, not the law.
comments.comment: Therefore also those being baptized, as if dying to bodily citizenships, imitate the pure conduct in the heavens and join themselves according to the heart to God. If anyone lives in Christ and is baptized, this one is a new creation (2 Cor 5:17), no longer living according to the law but according to the new grace of the Spirit.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The old things that passed away are either the legal and prophetic writings, read now through the gospel, or the customs before faith, and in both cases all things are from God.
comments.comment:
Having believed, the old things have passed away, having grown old as the new things come into the midst. And if he says the old things are the legal and prophetic writings, these have passed away because of the gospels having received them; regarding these old and new things, the difference is not according to their underlying substance but by way of thought; for the very same teaching of the two covenants has happened at one time concealed and at another time nakedly. The concealed things are therefore old.

And if anyone says that the customs and state of affairs before faith are old, these have passed away, having ceased, because the teaching according to the gospel has established itself. Regarding the former explanation, all things will fit from God, for both the law and the prophets and the gospels are from God; according to the later narrative, all the new things are from God, and not indeed even those that have passed away.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The time of the Savior's coming is a new age that remakes what was growing old, and we live no longer in the Mosaic manner but in the gospel life.
comments.comment: For the season of our Savior’s sojourn is a new age for us, transferring all things toward the better and thoroughly remaking into the newness of creation what was growing old and near vanishing. (Heb 8:13) ‘If anyone is in Christ — a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, they have become new.’ (2 Cor 5:17) And we ourselves no longer live in the Mosaic manner, but have been carried over into evangelical life, Christ renewing us through the Spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 17

comments.capsule: Being in Christ is a new creation because the curse of the law and the old ways have passed away, and all things are from God, who reconciled us through Christ.
comments.comment:
“So if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation,” he says; “the old things have passed away; behold, they have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

For the old is the saying, “Earth you are, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3:19), and also that word in the book of Moses, “For the mind of man is intently set on evil from his youth” (Genesis 8:21). Old as well, besides these, are the things in the law. All these, he says, have passed away; for we have been justified through faith in Christ, and the power of the curse has ceased. He who trampled the might of death came back to life for us, and we have come to know Him who is God by nature and in truth, as we fulfil the worship in spirit and in truth (John 4:23–24), while the Son mediates and gives the world the blessings from above and from the Father. Hence the inspired Paul says very wisely: “All things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:18). For truly, the mystery of the economy in the flesh, and the renewal made through Him, are not against the Father’s will.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'old things' are that have passed away.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We were enemies held by error and sins, but God reconciled us through the Lord who died and rose, and gave the apostles the teaching on reconciliation so that the friendship might last.
comments.comment: And all things are from God, the one who reconciled us to himself through Christ. For we were enemies, held fast by error and sins, but we have been reconciled to him, having received forgiveness toward him and through him; and he reconciled us to himself through the Lord who died and rose on our behalf. So that we might not become insensitive to the great goodness of God, he gave the teaching concerning the reconciliation to the apostles, so that being instructed by them we might remain in the being-in-Christ; for through him the friendship toward God which came to be after the reconciliation will persist.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain words what the reconciliation is and why it was entrusted to the apostles.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Father reconciled both Greeks, made enemies by many gods, and Jews, fastened to the shadows of the law, through Christ, who is the way to the Father.
comments.comment: Our guide into the mysteries adds to this that the Father Himself reconciled us to Himself through Christ: us Greeks, who had been made His enemies by straying into the worship of many gods, and Jews, by wishing to stay fastened to the shadows of the law and not accepting the message of true worship. For through Him we have obtained access (Ephesians 2:18), and “no one comes to the Father,” as He Himself says, “except through” Him (John 14:6). So “all things are from God, who reconciled us through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:18).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The preaching is a ministry of reconciliation, and "God was in Christ reconciling the world" means that God reconciled it through Christ.
comments.comment: … He says the proclamation is a ministry of reconciliation, through which believing ones shall be reconciled to God (2 Cor 5:18-19). Thus it must be understood: that God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ. Thus then it must be grasped: that God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, which is to say through Christ (2 Cor 5:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'God was in Christ' in plain words.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Though Christ gave the apostles their ministry of reconciliation, Paul says God gave it, showing that Christ is God, who in the person of Christ forgives and reconciles the world.
comments.comment: Notice again, I ask you, that although it was Christ who gave them the ministry of reconciliation, for they were appointed to apostleship through Him, he said that God was the giver. So they proclaim Him God, equal in glory to the Father, knowing that the two have one lordship and authority. What sort, then, is this word concerning the ministry, or what is the manner of the reconciliation? He goes on to say: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19), that is, He who was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ was God. For through faith in Christ, as I said, we have made peace with God (Romans 5:1), that is, we have been reconciled. And a clear proof of this is the forgiveness of our offences, which the God and Father grants; and the Son in turn, as God, extends it with authority, saying to the paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9:2; Luke 5:20). So “in Christ,” that is, in the person of Christ, God reconciles the world to Himself, “not counting” their trespasses against those who have sinned (2 Corinthians 5:19).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Appointed to the ministry of reconciliation, the apostles take Christ's person and plead with those who drift away to be reconciled to God by believing in Christ, the door and the way.
comments.comment: Since, he says, we have been appointed to the sacred service of the gospel’s decrees, and the word of reconciliation has been placed in us (2 Corinthians 5:19), for we are God’s ministers (2 Corinthians 6:4), we must make entreaties to those who have believed in this way, for their own sake; and, taking up as it were the very person of Christ, we say to those who wish to drift away: “We beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20), by believing in Him, that is, clearly, in the One on whose behalf we are ambassadors. For Christ is the door (John 10:9), and He Himself is the way (John 14:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be an ambassador for Christ.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The apostles are ambassadors in Christ's place, and God pleads through them as through Christ, because they are His ministers and servants.
comments.comment: Now we are ambassadors instead of Christ, entreating you by God through us (2 Cor 5:20). Then also he shows that he is grieved because of those keeping the law; for on account of Christ, he says, not on account of the law (2 Cor 5:20). And God entreats through us as through Christ, of whom we are ministers and servants (2 Cor 5:20).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul calls the apostles ambassadors for Christ through whom God appeals, so that Christ is God, and being reconciled to Him is being reconciled to God.
comments.comment: “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were appealing through us; we beg on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God.” (2 Corinthians 5:20) Notice: they are ambassadors for Christ, and they say God appeals to us. Then again they say, “We beg on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God.” Therefore Christ is God; when we have been reconciled to him, we have been reconciled to God.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Christ was made "sin" in the sense of a sin offering, as under the law of Moses, without committing sin, and was condemned with sinners so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him.
comments.comment:
And he says of the God and Father: “Him who knew no sin He made sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him” (2 Corinthians 5:21). It is as if he were saying: He caused the One who had never sinned at all to suffer the lot of those who greatly love sin, so that He might show us, who have received faith in Him, to be righteous. For He endured “the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2); for One died for all (2 Corinthians 5:14), He whose worth equals that of all.

So when He is said to have become sin, do not suppose that He committed sin; for the Word, being God, does not know how to do wrong. Know rather that He was given by the God and Father for our sins, just as, under the law of Moses, they called the victims slain for sin “sins.” At any rate it is written in the prophets about those appointed to serve as priests: “They will eat the sins of My people, and in their iniquities they will take their souls” (Hosea 4:8). For under the law the overseers and ministers of the divine altars ate the sacrifices offered for sins.

It is a great means, then, of shaming those who would be careless, to ponder wisely that He who did not know sin was condemned with sinners and hung beside them for our sake, so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him (2 Corinthians 5:21). For we have been justified by the God and Father “not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to His great mercy” (Titus 3:5), through faith in Christ.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that 'made sin' does not mean Christ sinned, using the law's sin offerings.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: "The one not knowing sin" means not tempted by it, not ignorant of its nature, for the Savior knew all things.
comments.comment: Regarding 2 Cor 5:21, they say 'the one not knowing' instead of 'the one not having been tempted by sin'; for he does not say not to be ignorant of its nature—rather the Savior knew it all things—but rather not to be tempted by it. For so also the one guarding the commandment will not know an evil word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To "know" in Scripture can mean to have experienced and been united to something, so Christ "did not know sin" by not having practiced it.
comments.comment: To know in the Scripture does not always signify merely to have certain knowledge, but also to have experienced something and to be united to it, as in: 'not knowing sin' (2 Corinthians 5:21), and: 'I never knew you, workers of lawlessness' (Matthew 7:23); for he did not know sin as in not having certain knowledge of what sin is, but as in not having practiced it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that 'knew no sin' means Christ never practiced sin, not that he did not understand it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ became a curse to loose the curse, and "sin" so that those once mastered by sin might become the righteousness of God.
comments.comment: And just as one becoming a curse looses the curse so as to provide a blessing in its place—for we say he became under a curse not so that he might suffer, but so that he might loose the curse and extend a blessing in its place—so too, he did not make sin for us who did not know sin, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him (cf. 2 Cor 5:21). Sin becomes the means by which those having righteousness are made righteousness. It is not called sin simply, but sin for the purpose of making those previously mastered by sin righteousness, not simply, but the righteousness of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Keeping the law made us sinners, but Christ became sin to deliver us from sin.
comments.comment: He showed from here how he is grieved because of those striving who keep the law; for keeping the law, he says, we have become sinners (2 Cor 5:21). Christ has become sin, so that he might deliver us from sin (2 Cor 5:21).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Believers are to receive the reconciliation, and the apostles may cooperate and suffer with them toward salvation.
comments.comment:
And God provided these things; receive the reconciliation, turning away from keeping the legalities (2 Cor 6:1).

It was permitted to the apostles not only to entreat but also to cooperate and suffer with them toward salvation, so that they might sincerely receive the grace from God (2 Corinthians 6:1).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ's mystery shone forth at the time God willed, and the day of salvation Paul speaks of is the time of the incarnation.
comments.comment: “In an acceptable time I have listened to you, and on a day of salvation I have helped you” (Isaiah 49:8). Christ and His mystery were foreknown before the foundation of the world (1 Peter 1:20), but they shone forth at the times the Sovereign willed, the times at which He has helped us; and the time of the incarnation he calls a day of salvation. So too, somewhere, the divine Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'now is the day of salvation' as the time of the incarnation.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The acceptable time was fulfilled when the Savior came at the consummation of the ages, when all had sinned, to taste death for everyone.
comments.comment: Paul also writes that this time was fulfilled when the Savior came, saying, “Behold, now is the acceptable time” (2 Corinthians 6:2). For properly the Savior’s descent also happened, he having shone forth at the consummation of the ages. For since the Savior came to take away the sin of the world, it was not fitting that so great a one should come and suffer for few sinners. When the time stood apart in which it is said, “All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23), and there was no longer a righteous person on earth who understood and sought after God, he came who by the grace of God tastes death for everyone on behalf of all of them.
comments.author: Apollinaris of Laodicea

comments.capsule: God helped at an acceptable time by giving up His Son, so we must commend ourselves by good works, free of blame.
