comments.comment: Regarding 2 Cor 6:2, 'Since God helped, having heard in an acceptable time and a day of salvation, having sent his own Son and having given him up on our behalf, so that no stumbling block of unbelief might come against anyone, so that the ministry of the evangelical teaching might not incur blame.' Therefore, it is necessary to be diligent in recommending oneself through good works, even if it be with toil.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The ministry is commended through honor and dishonor, good report and evil report.
comments.comment: Let no stumbling-block be given, that the ministry be not blamed, but in all things commending: through honor won by confession and dishonor borne from torturers, through good report of angels and evil report of men — deceivers in persecutors' eyes, true before God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Endurance is the foundation for facing trials.
comments.comment: As an unbreakable foundation, endurance is pre-laid, which enduring, it is easy to face every trial (2 Corinthians 6:4).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Endurance in tribulations, necessities and bonds, with right thinking and the fear of the Lord, brings purity of soul.
comments.comment: [Commending oneself:] This happens if, having endurance, we bear tribulations, necessities, distresses, and the surrounding things bravely, cheerfully bearing the experience of bonds and prison. For thus to be pure according to the soul will happen to one thinking rightly and acting rightly; for our souls, he says, having become pure in the obedience of the truth. But also the fear of the Lord, being pure, acquires all purity for the one who has received it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The left weapons of righteousness belong to one justified by the shadow of the law, the right weapons to one persuaded by the righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ.
comments.comment:
He says that there are right and left weapons of righteousness (2 Cor 6:7). … In other writings it is said, concerning putting on the weapons of light. These weapons of the warfare are not fleshly, that is, not human, but they turn out to be powerful for God.

Know if you are able to have the more leftward weapons of righteousness, the one being justified according to the shadow of the law; but the right weapons, the one having been persuaded according to the righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ for all who believe. And this is that about which the Savior said to the disciples: unless your righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall by no means enter the kingdom of heaven (Matt 5:20).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The right hand of righteousness does good and the left avoids evil, and both glory and dishonor come from those who receive or insult the word.
comments.comment: The weapons of righteousness: the right hand to do good works, and the left to avoid evil deeds, and through both of these righteousness is established; for it is clear that when one is absent, the other becomes idle (2 Cor 6:7). Through the glory, indeed, of those receiving the word and marveling at it, and through the dishonor of those insulting the believing ones; and the same word is also regarding the following (2 Cor 6:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left'.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul has not constricted them with the saving teaching, since his heart and mouth are open, so they in return should widen their minds and receive it.
comments.comment: Having said 'do not be compressed in us', he teaches this: instead of 'we do not compress you with the saving teaching, nor shall there be a lack from us'; for our heart has been widened and our mouth has been opened for teaching (2 Cor 6:11-13). And you therefore, as in a response, widen your own mind and receive the teaching; for your heart has not been enlarged in such a way as to receive the teachings from me. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'our heart is wide open' and the call to widen theirs in return.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: As righteousness has no partnership with lawlessness, nor light with darkness, nor Christ with Beliar, the kingdom of sin cannot coexist with God's kingdom.
comments.comment: But concerning God's kingdom this too must be examined: that as there is no 'partnership of righteousness with lawlessness,' (2 Corinthians 6:14) nor 'fellowship of light with darkness,' nor 'concord of Christ with Beliar' — so the kingdom of sin cannot co-exist with God's kingdom. If, then, we wish to be ruled by God, let 'sin in no way reign in our mortal body,' (Romans 6:12) nor let us obey its commands, when it calls our soul to 'the works of the flesh' and things foreign to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the pairs of opposites in Paul's questions mean for how we live.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The law teaches in figures that those who cling to the guilty share their defilement, for a believer has no share with an unbeliever and light can make no terms with darkness.
comments.comment: But the law is spiritual (Romans 7:14), and once again it teaches us in figures that those who are guilty of the passions of the soul are unclean, charged with defilement; and those who touch them, or cling to them, are defiled together with them, clearly by the bond of a shared will or shared deeds. For ‘bad company ruins good character’ (1 Corinthians 15:33), and ‘a believer has no share with an unbeliever’ (2 Corinthians 6:15), and light is hostile to darkness and can make no terms with it (2 Corinthians 6:14).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Believers who are God's temple should stay apart from unbelievers and cleanse themselves, so that they may accomplish holiness.
comments.comment: Therefore, let us flee all these things previously mentioned, being temples of the spoken God; I will dwell in them and walk about in them. For if you become sons and daughters of God, set apart from the unclean unbelievers, do not lay yourselves under the same yoke so that you might happen to obtain these holy rewards, having cleansed yourselves from all defilements of the flesh arising from heterogamy [marriage to an unbeliever]; for then you will practically and in thinking accomplish holiness of the Spirit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Paul ties the cleansing in this verse to the promises just given.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Some read the verse as cleansing flesh and spirit, that is soul and mind, to accomplish holiness in the fear of the Lord.
comments.comment: The preceding word stands differently. For some read: 'Therefore, having these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, so that we may not have a defilement of sin from neither flesh nor spirit, that is, of the soul or of the mind; for then it will necessarily follow to accomplish in the fear of the Lord holiness, so as to be holy in spirit and body.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul commands that both flesh and spirit be cleansed, which shows that neither is evil in essence, and the cleansing is done in the fear of God out of obedience, not necessity.
comments.comment: The same Apostle writes to certain people in another Epistle: 'Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, accomplishing holiness in the fear of God' (2 Cor 7:1), showing also by this word how the flesh is able to be cleansed of the defilements of sin that attach to it. But also the spirit and the soul; for if the flesh were evil in essence, and the spirit were good in essence, then neither would the spirit have defilement, nor would the flesh be cleansed from defilement. But he commands both to be cleansed from defilement, saying also the manner of the cleansing. For, he says, accomplishing holiness in the fear of God. And it is well said: 'In the fear of God,' showing that they have obedience, and not out of necessity.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul names both flesh and spirit and how the cleansing happens.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Defilement is twofold, the flesh being stained by passions and the soul and mind by straying from sound faith and by deceits and quarrels.
comments.comment: Defilement in us is twofold, Palladius: of the flesh and of the spirit (2 Corinthians 7:1). The flesh is stained by its own outrageous and unholy passions; the soul and the mind are stained above all by straying from right doctrine to worse things and by the corruption of sound faith, and besides these by tricks and deceits, false oaths, gossip, conceit, quarrels, jealousies (2 Corinthians 12:20), and whatever lies near these and is akin to them and stands equally accused of wickedness.
comments.selected_reason: Spells out in plain terms what defilement of flesh and of spirit means.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 15

comments.capsule: Paul asks the Corinthians to make room for him, says he has wronged none of them, and speaks boldly without wishing to condemn them, being full of consolation and joy over them.
comments.comment: He who is about to speak with boldness along with those sending the letter, says to the Corinthians: 'Make room, that is, make space for us to be defending ourselves. We have become guilty of no injustice, nor corruption, nor greed toward any of you. And these things I speak with boldness, not desiring to condemn you; for I had testified that you are so ready as to die for us. And so are we for you; for such a readiness of purpose was prepared in our hearts and in yours. Therefore, having much boasting over you, I am full of consolation, the joy of your salvation and gladness overflowing in us…'
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain paraphrase of Paul's appeal and his claim of a clear conscience.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In Macedonia the flesh found no rest, yet the apostles took courage in the Spirit, and the battles without and fears within can be read either as persecutors and anxiety for wavering believers, or as outside attacks that leave the heart undisturbed while fear of falling away remains.
comments.comment:
For when we had come to Macedonia, our flesh had no respite from the constantly attacking trials. Yet even if the flesh has no rest, we take courage in the Spirit, since we are not hemmed in even when oppressed in every way.

Interpreting what those distressing things were, he brought forward that there were battles indeed from without, but fears from within. And this is understood in two ways: first, it must be said that there exist battles from without for the apostles from those wishing to persecute and influence, but fears from within for those within the church who seem to be steadfast and unshakeable; for they feared the instability of the Corinthians might waver, being quickly carried away from the doctrines of the truth, whence he says to them: 'I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve in his craftiness, your minds be corrupted' (2 Cor 11:3). Otherwise, 'fightings without' might be understood as this: that the uprisings against us are occurring; those from without afflict us, yet do not advance so far as to trouble the heart. However, even if the soul is undisturbed, there are fears within concerning falling away; for we are liable to fall away.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Beside the war from outside there were scandals and rivalries among the faithful, and this inner war was harsher, since Paul feared the falls of his own people more than the plots of enemies.
comments.comment: And this was not the only difficulty—that a great and unceasing war was stirred up from outside—but also among the faithful themselves there happened to be scandals, strifes, rivalries, and jealousies. Paul made this clear when he said, “Outside are battles, within are fears” (2 Corinthians 7:5). And this war was harsher than the other, both for those being led and for the teachers. Paul did not fear the plots of enemies as much as he feared the falls within and the transgressions of his own people.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the inward fears were and why they weighed on Paul.
comments.author: John Chrysostom
comments.work: On the Resurrection of the Dead

comments.capsule: God comforts the humble, and Paul was comforted by Titus both in person and by his report that the Corinthians' brief sorrow over the letter had become a seed of joy.
comments.comment: God, who shows grace to the humble, comforts them, offering encouragement, so that they may bear the heavy things with endurance (2 Cor 7:6); he also comforted us by the arrival of Titus from you to us (2 Cor 7:7). And it was not his presence alone that comforted, but also his report concerning you; for he told of the godly zeal you showed him. He also extended to us, who know his gladness, the news of how surpassingly he keeps his affection and compassion for you. You have zeal and lamentation and longing on my behalf, so that I no longer doubt that you have left behind the rebukes of the former letter; for I learned from his words that the sorrow, having existed for a little while from what was written, has become a seed and the greatest occasion for joy (2 Corinthians 7:8).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Titus's coming and report comforted Paul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Silence would have left them ungrieved and unrepentant, so Paul rejoices in a grief that is spiritual.
comments.comment: For if I kept silent, he says, and did not strike, you were not grieved; but if you were not grieved, you would have been harmed if you were not repenting. I rejoice, he says, over your afflictions, because they are not worldly but spiritual.
comments.selected_reason: Shows why Paul can rejoice that the letter grieved them.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul wrote so that the Corinthians' zeal would be known, and since they grieved according to God and repented, he rejoices and is confident in them.
comments.comment: It must be sought, not for their sake, but so that your zeal may be known through the spoken word having been inscribed for the purpose of obeying; for concerning this I always boast, exhorting the Macedonians to the same zeal. Indeed, it was necessary, so that I might not be ashamed of you having received sorrow not properly. Since therefore it did not happen so, but according to God you having grieved, as much as much, followed by repentance, I rejoice and am confident in all such things in you.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Godly sorrow that works repentance differs from worldly sorrow, whose groaning is destructive.
comments.comment: This groaning corresponds to 'the sorrow that works repentance unto salvation' (2 Corinthians 7:10). This sorrow is another from that of the world, which works death. If, indeed, you see a man groaning because he does not attain what he desires, even if they are bad things, this groaning is destructive.
comments.selected_reason: Distinguishes godly from worldly sorrow in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Godly sorrow works an unchangeable repentance unto salvation, so worldly sorrow is to be rejected.
comments.comment: Working out an unchangeable salvation through pains brought on pedagogically, about which the law-giving apostle Paul writes, marking these things: 'The godly sorrow works out unchangeable repentance unto salvation, bringing about the death of the sorrow of the world' (2 Cor 7:10). Therefore, this worldly sorrow must be rejected, but the godly one must be unchangeably opposed, bringing about salvation according to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wrongdoer is the man who took his father's wife; the one wronged is the father or the law.
comments.comment: By 'the one who did wrong' he means the man who had taken his father's wife, and by 'the one wronged' either the father — whose wife he had taken, even if the father is dead — or the law that forbids such a marriage (2 Cor 7:12).
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly who is meant by the wrongdoer and the one wronged.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul wrote to show the Corinthians' eagerness and obedience, and he was refreshed by it.
comments.comment: But as it seems and as the outcome showed, not because of this I wrote, but so that your eagerness and your obedience might be shown; … In this he has been refreshed, because they were obeying his teaching.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Titus's witness to the Corinthians' obedience increased Paul's joy, because the spirit finds rest when the rest comes by piety and virtue and not by fleshly pleasure.
comments.comment:
Through this joy, our encouragement and consolation were increased, with Titus testifying concerning your zeal with holiness (2 Cor 7:13-15), for he says the spirit rests from your obedience, especially since he found it so, just as I always announced to him concerning your obedience. The spirit rests somewhat when, from those who are the causes of rest, one receives according to piety and virtue and a faithful mindset according to the truth, those who receive the pleasant things of life from those who gladden, resting according to the flesh and not according to the spirit.

For Titus constantly restores us by announcing your beautiful obedience …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Persecuted and poor, the Macedonians rejoiced the more and became bountiful, to stir the Corinthians.
comments.comment: In which, he says, they are greatly afflicted being persecuted, in this they rejoice more, and their poverty according to the depth overflowed into the wealth of their generosity. And the apostle testifies to the Macedonians that being poor they became bountiful in well-doing, so that also the Corinthians might be stirred toward fruitfulness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse about the Macedonians' joy and poverty overflowing in generosity.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Macedonian eagerness moved Paul to send Titus to Corinth.
comments.comment: The eagerness of the Macedonians toward well-doing prompted us to entreat Titus to come to you, so that he might also prompt you toward fruitfulness.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the reason Paul sent Titus to Corinth.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Christ became poor for others without casting away his wealth, as he took a slave's form without casting away God's form.
comments.comment: And behold the difference: “know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that being rich he became poor for your sakes” (2 Cor 8:9). To become poor for us, is not to be rich for us; for it has not been said to become rich just as it has been said to become poor, but “being rich he became poor for your sakes.” And just as having the form of God and being in the form of God, having taken the form of a slave of God, he did not cast away the form of God, so he, becoming poor for the sake of others, did not cast away the wealth; … Thus, remaining rich, he became poor. But he became poor for the sake of others, so that they might become rich.
comments.selected_reason: Shows what it means that Christ, being rich, became poor.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Word, rich as God, willingly became poor and took our nature so that human nature might rise to the heights and put away the shame of poverty.
comments.comment: Rich as God, he willingly became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9) and became as we are, so that human nature, having come in Christ into the heights of divine superiority, might put away the shame of poverty. For God the Father raised us together in Christ and seated us together in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), as it is written. But we would not have come into these things if the One who is rich as God had not clothed himself with the nature that is poor. A human who is poor by his own nature would not “become poor”; that befits more fittingly the One who is truly rich — that is, the Word from God the Father — when he became as we are.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says Christ became poor and what that gains for us.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Giving is willing and according to what one has, and exchanging earthly for spiritual gifts brings equality.
comments.comment: The word of piety does not compel one to give what one does not have, but what one has should be provided willingly (2 Cor 8:10-15). And this will be easily accomplished when they see who are the partakers; for these are holy and God's healers. Therefore we also hope that an exchange will be; for they are sufficient to provide spiritual things instead of the sensible things they receive. For thus equality will be even in the present time, as it happened during the giving of the manna, neither the one having little being diminished nor the one having much exceeding; for inequality remains when, those having heavenly things of the saints, and you having earthly things, no exchange takes place. Therefore, sow carnal things, participating in the needs of the saints, so that you may reap from them the spiritual; for thus there will be equality in your receiving from the great and from those who are small; for you shall have the great things with the small, and they the small things with the great. And this equality will exist according to restorative justice.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Accept what is offered when in need and give to the lacking when abounding, which is the equality Paul meant.
comments.comment: If food or clothing is needed, do not be ashamed to receive those things offered to you by others. For this is a form of pride. But if you yourself abound in these things, give to the one lacking. In this way God wants to manage His own children. For this reason also the Apostle, writing to the Corinthians, was saying concerning the lacking ones: 'That your abundance may be for their lack, so that their abundance may also be for your lack, so that equality may occur, just as it has been written: He who has much, did not increase, and he who has little, did not diminish' (2 Cor 8:14-15).
comments.selected_reason: Applies Paul's call for equality to everyday giving and receiving.
comments.author: Evagrius Ponticus

comments.capsule: Paul sent the brother so that no one could blame the giving before men.
comments.comment: This joining to the fact that we sent along the brother, whose praise is in the gospel, … lest anyone should blame us as hindering the well-doing toward the saints. Before the Lord it is good to serve in well-doing, and before men not to be blamed and slandered in the vigor of the ministry.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The cheerful giver rejoices in giving and shares without grumbling or grief.
comments.comment: The apostle's word is good: "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7)—one who rejoices in giving and does not sow sparingly, so that he may not reap in the same way; one who shares without grumbling, division, or grief, which is pure beneficence.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what a cheerful giver is in plain terms.
comments.author: Clement of Alexandria
comments.work: Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?

comments.capsule: Paul urges gentleness on them because the Corinthians were stirred up against opponents, which is far from the meekness of Christ whom he sets before them.
comments.comment:
Many of the wise men of Athens lived among the people of Corinth. They regarded the Savior’s cross as foolishness (1 Corinthians 1:23), and they called the blessed Paul himself, the herald of the word of inspired Scripture, a charlatan and a babbler (Acts 17:18), together with the other saints. Some others of the circumcision, in turn, were setting upon the believers, praising circumcision and the sacrifices of the law, and saying that the blessed Paul was out of his mind, as one who had impiously chosen to make war on the ancient decrees. Against such men the zealous among the Corinthians were stirred up, and quite naturally; they wanted to lay hands on them as enemies of the divine preaching.

But the thing was most unseemly, and as far as could be from the gentleness that befits saints; for, as it is written, “the Lord’s servant must not quarrel, but be kind to all, correcting his opponents with meekness” (2 Timothy 2:24–25). So he gives them a charge, saying: I, Paul myself, the priest of the divine mysteries, the steward and apostle, the one renowned for zeal, who spur you yourselves on to say with me, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21), entreat you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, “who when He was reviled did not revile in return, when He suffered did not threaten, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23). So at the right moment he brings them to remember the life of Christ, and makes them most meek and gentle.

I, Paul myself, he says, who am lowly when present among you face to face, not haughty, nor sharpened for quarrels and fights; who am bold when absent, I ask even now that when present I may not have to be bold (2 Corinthians 10:1–2). For, as I am minded to think, you will by no means take bold action against certain people who think that we walk, as it were, according to the flesh, that is, live in a fleshly way, in strife and jealousy. For, he says, “where there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not fleshly, and walking in a human way?” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

Those, then, who wish to follow the Savior’s gentleness ought to rise above the suspicion of those men and not walk in a fleshly way.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the setting of Paul's plea and what meekness means for readers, without needing a controversy.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul asks for their obedience so that he need not come as a stern teacher, and he says God knows his counsel was given only for the good of the ministry.
comments.comment: I, myself, your teacher, writing on the matter at hand, urge you — by the virtue Christ has given me, that is, gentleness and forbearance (2 Cor 10:1) — to take courage, though I am still far from your obedience, so as not to seem lowly when present; for when I come and find you turning my exhortation into deeds, I will dwell with you in a moderate spirit, with much gentleness (2 Cor 10:2). Therefore I beg that I may not, when present, have to be so bold as to wear the face of a teacher who rebukes and strikes — lest I be forced, with a teacher's frank confidence, to act boldly against some who suppose that we walk according to the flesh. Or would anyone decline to suppose that we walk according to the flesh, if he supposes that we wrote this not for the cause itself but to be thought great men — while you yourselves prove obedient and contribute even more? For God testifies — and most men with him — that this counsel was given so that the ministry might abound, and not for any other human end (2 Cor 10:3).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Walking in the flesh means living on earth, while not warring after the flesh is having our citizenship in heaven.
comments.comment: The present passage means what is written in another letter: 'Though we walk on earth, our citizenship is in heaven' (Phil 3:20); for walking 'according to the flesh' is the same as walking 'on earth' — and, conversely, not warring 'according to the flesh' is having our citizenship in heaven (2 Corinthians 10:3).
comments.selected_reason: Makes clear what 'walking in the flesh' but not 'warring according to the flesh' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Soldiers of this world use fleshly armour, but the Christian soldier fights with the spiritual armour Paul names in Ephesians.
comments.comment:
“For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh; for the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful through God” (2 Corinthians 10:3–4).

Those who know how to win renown in battle, and who rise against their enemies in a fleshly way, would quite naturally have fleshly armour; for they have helmets and breastplates, weapons and swords, and all the things by which they could conquer. But our wrestling and our manner of warfare need spiritual weapons (Ephesians 6:12). Indeed, the inspired Paul says very well that the one who is counted a soldier in Christ must be adorned with such splendid armour. He puts on him righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet, “and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God,” and besides these “the shield of faith,” by which all the flaming arrows of the evil one are quenched (Ephesians 6:14–17).
comments.selected_reason: Shows what the 'weapons not of the flesh' are, with Paul's own list of armour.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The weapons of the Christian are spiritual, and with them he pulls down the proud arguments that people think cannot be overthrown.
comments.comment:
For certainly, the weapons they carry are not perceptible and bodily—for these are weak—but they are powerful to God. For those using these things cast down the strongholds of the deceitful words most sophistically constructed by the heterodox, and also the things exalted in these words against the knowledge of God. For those opposing the knowledge of truth, introducing impious and atheistic doctrines, building strong fortresses with the intensity of words, and finding space within them, think they are invincible. …

Therefore, in order to cast down the aforementioned exaltations and strongholds, having put on the armor of God according to the spirit, we fight in the said manner. For we dissolve their sophistic words and refute their doctrines.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'strongholds' and 'high things' are: arguments that think themselves unbeatable.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints' war is mental rather than bodily, fought with the weapons of truth against twisted reasonings about God.
comments.comment: “For the weapons of our campaign are not fleshly, but powerful with God for the tearing down of strongholds, tearing down reasonings and every height raised against the knowledge of God, and taking every thought captive into the obedience of Christ.” (2 Corinthians 10:4–5) The saints’ war is not thick and bodily, but rather lean and mental. For they are accustomed to succeed not by moving fleshly weapons… but fitted with the weapons of the truth, rising up spiritually… against those who want to mis-mark it and twist the straightness of the divine doctrines… So the saints’ weapons are not fleshly, but rather powerful with God. For they tear down reasonings that carry us off into outlandish thoughts… and if someone should lift a horn high among those who habitually speak injustice against God, they all but strike him down with thoughts toward straightness, turning him to the right path and setting him into the words of the truth.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: The saints' arrows are spiritual and are used to pull down proud ideas about God and to bring others onto the right path.
comments.comment: So the arrows of the saints are not fleshly but rather spiritual and powerful through God, useful for pulling down strongholds (2 Corinthians 10:4), I mean the doctrines of the Greeks and of the heretics, and for showing their arguments to be rotten, utterly unskilful, and senselessly put together. “Let us then pull down such things, and every high thing raised up against the knowledge of God; and we shall take every thought captive to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5). That is to say: let us pull down every height of impious notions raised up against God, and glorify Him with fitting words, imagining nothing lowly about Him. For we shall benefit others too, bringing them onto the right and most unerring path of thought, so that we may punish all disobedience once our own obedience has first been fulfilled (2 Corinthians 10:6).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul brings every thought to obey Christ, as he turned the Athenian altar's inscription toward the one true God.
comments.comment: It is possible to take it also in this way: every thought brought in any teaching, we bring by necessity and force, relocating it toward persuading them to obey Christ. For just as the inscription lying on the altar in Athens shows the thought of many gods, he who writes these things has drawn it toward the only true God, saying: 'Whom not knowing, you worship; this I proclaim to you.' But the inscription showed a multitude of gods. … Therefore, when every thought is captured into obedience to Christ, we will be ready to bring such a thing as a vengeance against all disobedience …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a concrete example of taking a thought captive: Paul's use of the Athenian altar.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul was ready to punish disobedience but did not want to use the sword at once.
comments.comment: And having readiness to avenge every disobedience, when your obedience is fulfilled. Because I knew that some are persuaded by speech and exhortation, I was not willing immediately to use the sword, as I consider against some, since they did not seem to be obeying by speech alone.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul rebukes them for judging by outward show, not works.
comments.comment: This must be read with reproachful hypocrisy: you take your examination not from works—that is, from the truth—but simply from what appears on the surface (2 Corinthians 10:7).
comments.author: Gennadius of Constantinople
comments.work: Fragments on the First and Second Epistles to the Corinthians

comments.capsule: Paul says to judge each person by his conduct, so that reputation does not hide the truth.
comments.comment: Test accurately each one according to the worthiness of the face's conduct (2 Cor 10:7). This he sees regarding the apostles; for since it was destined to reprove those from circumcision, and they were putting forward Peter and James and John, be certain, he says, lest the status of faces might ever prevent you from perceiving the truth.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul's words can be read as a command or as a statement, and the first reading teaches them to test teachers by what they truly are.
comments.comment: He brings these things to bear against those whom he was writing to: 'when your obedience is fulfilled, look to the outward appearance.' There is a difference in understanding this word: if it were expressed commandingly, it would mean this: if, O Corinthians, your obedience is fulfilled through agreement with the divine teaching, observe the outward appearance; for in this way you will know those who present themselves as sheep but are inwardly ravening wolves, and the truly genuine teachers, to whom it was said, 'You are the light of the world' (Matt 5:14). In this way, having observed, the impostors whom you also cast out will be known to you, as will the true apostles of Christ, in whom you also desired to believe willingly. This agrees with 'by their fruits you will know them' (Matt 7:16). … Therefore, having doubt as to how 'look to the outward appearance' is expressed, the former understanding holds as the teaching.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who commend themselves measure themselves only against themselves, and next to others they are nothing.
comments.comment: We write these things not imitating those commending themselves—for this is not good (2 Cor 10:12)—for they do not perceive that they themselves measure themselves within themselves and are not able to compare themselves to another; for when compared to others they are nothing.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's point about self-commendation in simple terms.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul boasts only of the measure God allotted him, which reached as far as Corinth, and hopes to preach beyond them as their faith grows.
comments.comment: We do not boast beyond our measure as if we were superior to greater things (2 Cor 10:14); for even unto you we came and proclaimed the word (2 Corinthians 10:14). They boast of their own labors regarding our things, but we do not, but according to law we boast of the rule and the measure allotted to us, hoping to evangelize even beyond you as your faith increases. And he says 'rule' to mean reaching as far as them (2 Corinthians 10:15).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul's 'measure' and 'rule' are.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: If Paul boasts, it is through the Spirit's grace.
comments.comment: Even if we boast, it is not as if we were rectifying by our own wisdom, but by the grace of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 10:17).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The one approved is not the one who proves himself but the one the Lord has established, as the choice of the apostles shows.
comments.comment:
Having sufficiently refuted those teaching the opposite as if they were merely making a noise as Christ's, he necessarily brought forward that one must boast in the Lord, he who unblemishedly and sincerely relies on glory; for not he who proves himself to be approved is of such a kind in every way, but he whom the Lord has established through testimony. …

Indeed, he who writes the present things testified about him, saying to Ananias: 'This is for me a vessel of election.' But even to all the apostles, the election having come from the Savior testifies, that they themselves had not drawn themselves, but had received this from God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains verse 18: God, not self-praise, makes a man approved.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul asks them to bear with his boasting because he fears false teachers will destroy their simplicity as the serpent deceived Eve.
comments.comment: Having shown how it is the folly of the foolish to praise themselves, and that the Corinthians are rather led astray by such people, he says to them: 'I wish you would endure me speaking about myself what they also say about themselves; for having many true things to write, I requested not to, knowing that it seems foolish to talk about oneself. But since you endure those speaking thus, I will say also, not so that I may hunt praise, but that I may become a cause of benefit to you; for according to God I am zealous for you, not wishing that your minds should be destroyed by one of those saying evil things. And consequently I have the aforementioned zeal, since I was entrusted with the truth by the one true man, Christ, that your church is a pure virgin. It is necessary, lest you be destroyed also by false teachers through the integrity which you have, just as the serpent, using cunning, destroyed the mother of our race; … And someone will know that Eve was deceived by the cunning of the serpent, having understood how she misrepresented the divine commandment of God saying: "from every tree in the paradise and the following." For what was commanded in its entirety, she led away sophistically toward the opposing thing.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul fears for the Corinthians and how Eve's deception is the pattern.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A man who died to the law and was reborn in baptism is rightly called a pure virgin.
comments.comment: You died, he says, to the law, and have become another man, to the one risen from the dead. How then could a pure virgin have been previously married? But having been reborn through the bath of regeneration and having passed into another life, a pure virgin is justly so named. Faith in Christ and the brightness of the Spirit confirm the Christian life (2 Cor 11:4). If then you did not receive these things, you seek well those who still wish to live according to the law (2 Cor 11:10–12).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul's 'another Jesus' warns against honoring Christ as a mere man, when he is the Word of God made flesh.
comments.comment: “For if the one who comes proclaims another Jesus whom we did not proclaim, or you receive another spirit which you did not receive, or another gospel which you did not accept, you put up with it well enough.” (2 Corinthians 11:4) Before the times of the becoming-human, no one is found naming the Word from God “Jesus” or “Christ,” except by foreknowledge of what would be named in the times when he also became flesh. So the name Jesus is new to him when he became human. But if he is proclaimed as God, and as being one—for there is not another beside him whom some can proclaim—it is well, and we worship God; but if his measure is only that of the humanity, and he is honored with a bare union of persons, the word of our faith has been emptied, leading us to a human and not to God. But that is impious. Therefore Christ is God and Son, as the Word of God having become flesh (John 1:14).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Princesses Arcadia and Marina

comments.capsule: Paul asks if preaching free was a sin.
comments.comment: Or do you think that, having served the gospel to you for free, I sinned against myself by humbling myself?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul took nothing from them, and the brothers from Macedonia supplied his needs, so that he would burden no church.
comments.comment: And you know that not only when traveling away from you did I refrain from taking anything, but also when present among your mother-church, having been lacking because the necessary things were missing, I have not become a burden to other churches by having fulfilled their need; for indeed the brothers coming to me from Macedonia were providing for the needs. And this boldness is being preserved for me toward all the churches of Achaia; and I will guard this intention, so that in everything I may be without weight, just as I have kept myself and will keep myself.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's practice of taking no support and who supplied his needs.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul takes no pay so as to cut off the pretext of his accusers, and he blames only those who make the preaching a business.
comments.comment:
Not reproaching the Corinthians, he says this, but reproving those who use the preaching as a matter of commerce. Therefore he says that I do not stop boasting.

He means that I have not made the preaching a commercial venture like those; for I neither received anything from you nor do I receive, not as one not loving you—for I do love—but so that I might cut off the pretext of the accusers, so that whether they boast falsely or truly, they may be revealed just as we also are revealed (2 Corinthians 11:12).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul refuses support in Corinth.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul refuses payment so as to cut off every pretext of those looking for grounds to slander him.
comments.comment: For we do not do this out of a love for it, but so that we might cut off every pretense of those desiring to find occasions for slander, so that even if I seem to be refusing to take something from someone, the deceivers might be found just like us; for we are not like those, but they will be found to be like us (2 Cor 11:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The false workers are transformed into apostles of Christ in appearance only, as the devil himself pretends to be an angel of light.
comments.comment: But these, concerning whom I write, in one place are called deceitful workers, and in another letter they are named evil workers. They are transformed into apostles of Christ, not being such but deceiving by form alone, having the same disposition as the false prophets who, being wolves in thought, surround themselves with fleeces, so that they may be glorified as being sheep. Having said this about them, he shows that what has been said is not paradoxical; for if the cause of them being such happens to be—and this is the devil—he pretends to be an angel of light, while being of darkness, consequently those being led toward wandering with him transform themselves as to be received as pure, because they are ministers of righteousness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how deceivers pass as apostles, following the devil's own pretending.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Satan is darkness by nature and only pretends to be light, so he is not an angel of light in essence.
comments.comment: If anyone hears that the one being transformed is an angel of light, let him not suppose him to be such in essence—for this glory is Manichaean and impious—for the devil is evil and darkness by his own nature, and just as by his own choice he pretends to be light in order to be thought to have virtue and knowledge. Even if he thus deceives some by transforming into the aforementioned things, the end is appropriate for those doing them, going out with the devil into the eternal fire as his servants.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'transforms himself into an angel of light' does and does not mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul's 'foolishness' is not entirely foolish, since it is done for a wise purpose and is full of understanding.
comments.comment: The foolishness spoken here is not entirely such; for it is being accomplished economically, it is full of a most vigorous understanding. He gives this because, since many boast according to the flesh—'They are Hebrews, and Israelites, and the seed of Abraham; and I also' (2 Cor 11:22)—he precedes them in glory, that these things are spiritual (2 Cor 12:1-5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul shows how he shares the weakness and stumbling of others, saying he burns, not merely that he grieves.
comments.comment: “Who is weak,” he says, “and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29). He did not say, “and I am not grieved,” but “and I am not on fire,” wanting to show us by this term the intensity of the pain. And again, writing to others, he says, “You have begun to reign without us—and I wish you had begun to reign, so that we also might reign with you” (1 Corinthians 4:8). And again: “Now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 3:8). See how precious the good reputation of his brothers was to him—he did not even consider himself alive if they were not being saved.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Paul's 'I am not on fire' and how much he cared for his brothers.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Paul speaks of his visions as of another man, a man in Christ, because he was made worthy of them only by becoming in Christ, and Scripture shows that people can be taken up in the body.
comments.comment: He has come to report the God-sent visions and revelations that have existed, and while showing these to a great extent of divinity, he did not attribute them to himself, but as if reporting concerning another, arranging the boasts of weakness toward his own person. It is fitting, then, that he lifted up the indwelling vision to the man in Christ, in order to show that he was not worthy to be made such in any other way than having become in the Word of God, in wisdom, and in truth, and in sanctification; for all these things Christ is. This man in Christ was caught up to the third heaven and into paradise; whether in body or outside of this, I do not know. And one says that the written thing can be held in both ways: for Elijah was also caught up in a body, and Ambachum [Habakkuk] was taken up from Jerusalem to Babylon, carrying the body, having been moved by the counsel of an angel of God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul speaks of 'a man in Christ' and what being 'in the body or out of the body' could mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Someone still in the body can be led by the mind to heaven and paradise, or Paul may speak of his whole state, and God alone knows which.
comments.comment:
Regarding the heavenly ones, thus someone being surrounded by the body is still able to be guided by the vision of the mind in heaven and the paradise to become such.

Another will say that whether in a body or outside of a body, he writes not about his own body in which the soul is surrounded, but about the whole state, so that the thing said might be such: snatched up even to the third heaven and into the paradise (2 Cor 12:4). Whether these things are a body or incorporeal, I do not know; for the knowledge of these things rests with the Father of Wisdom, God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul's doubt whether he was in the body shows that the soul is not mortal, and the third heaven is the third of the expanse, with Paradise planted on earth in Eden.
comments.comment: … for if he had known it [the soul] was mortal, he would not have been wavering whether he saw the vision outside the body or in the body. And regarding the third heaven, he said the third of the expanse; for if he had ascended up to the three heavens, he certainly would have heard the unspeakable words there and not in Paradise. And let no one suppose Paradise to be above the heaven; for according to the east it is planted upon the earth in the place of Eden, whence also Adam was formed, as Moses recounts.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: The 'third heaven' may be counted from the firmament or be the third part of one heaven, and Paul was snatched up twice, to the third heaven and into paradise.
comments.comment: And the 'even to the third heaven' also contains ambiguity; for from the ambiguity it is signified whether, it being the case of the greater number of heavens, he reached up to the third to understand the things there—and let this be numbered from the firmament; for this is the first heaven for those being taken up entirely—or whether, it being the case of one heaven, he reached up to the third part of it. However it may be, God would know and whom He would himself make manifest; nevertheless, two snatchings are made evident: even to the third heaven and even into the paradise.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unutterable words are heard by the mind and not by syllables and sounds, and paradise is a school of divine lessons.
comments.comment:
However it may be, it is made evident that the paradise is a school of divine lessons.

And what does he intend by the unutterable words? Let it be known how much the one speaking them uses not syllables and sounds, being unutterable, compared to how much they have the truth, having the essence in divine intellect; and these things are heard not by the reception of sense but by the contemplation of divine intellect. For the God-Word Himself being Christ, does not neglect, speaking not to Paul but in Paul; and thus He also taught, becoming toward each of the prophets. If therefore the Savior speaks in the saints, the things said are unutterable; … For indeed it is possible for a man to hear, having an enlightened understanding, but it is impossible to speak those things with voices and syllables; for these are the speaking elements. 'Not within power' is said instead of 'possible'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul points to things beyond speech, not God alone, and 'heard' here means 'understood'.
comments.comment: We, however, say that not only God is beyond speech, but also other things that come after him. Paul, straining to point to these, says: “He heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter” (2 Corinthians 12:4). He uses “heard” in place of “understood”, as in the saying, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8; Matthew 11:15).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words Paul heard are unspoken because they come to the mind without syllables, yet they are words because they carry truth or falsehood.
comments.comment: This is why the divine apostle, knowing this, says 'he has heard unspoken words' (2 Corinthians 12:4). And it seems to be a contradiction, unless we take the spoken and the unspoken to mean something different from one another. They are unspoken insofar as they are spoken only in the mind, and God imparts them to the intellect. And they possess truth or falsehood, so that according to this also they are words. They are unspoken because they are not brought forth through syllables, not being able to be written or inscribed. But that which is not brought forth through syllables is unspoken. If, however, each of the things I say is spoken—for I bring it forth through articulated voice—yet the thought, which the voice does not submit, is an unspoken word. For it possesses either the truth or the lie. They are unspoken in that they do not have the quality of being brought forth through syllables and articulated words, but they are words in that they possess truth or falsehood.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how words can be 'unspeakable' yet still words: they come to the mind without syllables.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul boasts of the man in Christ who saw the visions but of himself only in weaknesses, so he is weak in himself and lifted high in Christ.
comments.comment: Having said this, he necessarily brought forward the divine revelations and visions: 'I will boast about a man such as this being in Christ, but about myself I speak boldly only concerning the aforementioned weaknesses' (2 Corinthians 12:5). And he who says these things is not another from the one who has seen the visions; except if he is indeed the same, he differs in thought—how indeed he is understood as a weak man because of the intention of the condescension, but how he is understood as having ascended super-eminently and being in Christ because of the vision.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul boasts of 'a man' but only of his own weaknesses.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The thorn is not a bodily ailment, as many suppose, but persecutions that came from the devil's working through a Satanic angel.
comments.comment:
And he speaks of persecutions as weaknesses, not a bodily passion as some suppose (2 Cor 12:7).

It is suspected by many as having a pain around the head, but the truth is he speaks of persecutions, since the temptations came from a diabolical energy. And he called the one serving the temptation to the devil a Satanic angel, from a transformation of the angels serving God.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: A man given great visions might think highly of himself, so Paul was allowed to be afflicted and fled to God in prayer.
comments.comment:
Others … will say: 'Someone having received many and great visions, if he were not overcome by human weakness, would think greatly of himself.' In order that he might not have room, the power guarding the ruling principle of God often manages for the one being guarded to be outside the protection of it, so that they might slip in and take a human thought.

And since perfect men shut out even the contamination in the intellect, they think they have a great disaster, even if a memory is cast upon them by a satanic angel. Therefore, they indeed entreat to be cleansed also from secret things and to not have any awareness of something trivial. And that this is so, he knew, being afflicted, to flee to God, as he shows having written: 'Concerning this distressing satanic angel, three times I entreated the Lord, so that he might be removed from me.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul's thorn was not a bodily illness but the human opponents who served the devil and scourged his flesh while his soul was lifted up by hope.
comments.comment: So, growing weary and no longer bearing the assaults of enemies who were constantly cutting short his teaching and opposing his word, he falls before the Master and pleads with him, saying: “A thorn in the flesh was given to me, a messenger of Satan, to strike me. Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). I know that some think this weakness is bodily—but it is not, it is not. He calls the opposing human beings a messenger of Satan. For “Satan” is a Hebrew word, and “Satan” means “the one who opposes.” So he calls the instruments of the devil, the human beings who serve him, his messengers. Why then, he says, is it attached to the flesh? Because the flesh was being scourged, while the soul was being lifted up, raised high by hope in the things to come. For it did not touch the soul, nor did it trip up the reasoning within; the devices and the war stopped at the flesh, unable to pass inside.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'thorn in the flesh' as the persecutions Paul suffered.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Because Paul had much to be proud of, the Father gave him an angel of Satan to buffet him so that he would not be exalted.
comments.comment: Paul had the material for exaltation through visions, through sights, through wonders and signs, through the toils he toiled for Christ, through the churches he planted, ambitious where Christ was not named to found a church. All these were material for him, if one must speak with the semblance about exaltation, that to some it would have seemed fine for him to exalt himself. But still, since even exaltation over such things is not without danger, the kind Father, as he granted him visions and sights, so also gave him in the portion of a gift 'an angel of Satan to buffet him, that he may not be exalted beyond measure.' (2 Corinthians 12:7) And about this he begged the Lord three times that the angel of Satan depart from him—the one given him that he may not exalt himself. And the Lord answered him (for Paul was worthy of the Lord's answer) and said to him: 'My grace is enough for you; for my power is perfected in weakness.' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the thorn was given: to keep Paul from being exalted.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The power given is perfected in persecutions and tribulations.
comments.comment: You have an apostolic grace; do not seek this and succeed even without temptations; for my power is perfected in persecutions and tribulations (2 Corinthians 12:9).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul asks pardon if they think his taking nothing wrong.
comments.comment: If then you have nothing to accuse me of, that I, having desisted from seeking sustenance despite the need, received nothing from you, in which even if you think I have sinned, forgive me and grant me grace for this injustice which you think is being done by me (2 Corinthians 12:13).
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: Paul is not defending himself to them, since he has always aimed to please God and to persuade men rightly, and he hopes they will give up whispering and quarrels.
comments.comment: Do not think that we are defending ourselves to you (2 Cor 12:19); for we have not previously been set to please men, but God (2 Corinthians 12:19). We intend good things before God and also before men, so that we may be revealed to God, persuading men rightly by life and fitting speech; for speaking in Christ, we are additionally speaking for God, as seeing His purpose, we do all things and say all things. Therefore, I am confident that having read this letter sincerely, you will depart from whispering, having rejected it as slave-like; for the boldness of slaves is in muttering and grumbling. But also turn away from contentions and the quarrels arising from them and from ambition; for thus it will follow that you find what you desire.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul says he is not defending himself, and what he asks of them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A teacher is humbled when those he taught need rebuke, and he should mourn those who are dead in soul.
comments.comment: For a teacher who is prosperous in listeners, in whom he can speak wisdom, is tossed about and greatly puffed up, but is immediately humbled when those approaching need reproof and conviction regarding what they are doing badly. For if they practice fornication and uncleanness and the following debauchery and do not repent, they have died the death of the soul; so that one having a nurturing disposition toward them should rather mourn them than those building empty tombs for those who have departed from philosophy. For sensation loves to be near to those sinning, when others mourn for them with wailing. The Savior is able even according to this to bless those who mourn, since after the evil from mourning they shall be comforted by God. But because he says 'lest coming again I be humbled' (2 Corinthians 12:21), he shows that even previously he has sufficiently experienced this toward them, having turned them toward repentance.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Being humbled for a teacher means seeing those he taught fall, whereas he would be lifted up by their progress.
comments.comment: But do you wish to know that the descent upon one sinning is humiliation? Paul writes to the Corinthians, stirring them up toward repentance, he says: 'Lest coming I should find you and my God should humble me' (2 Corinthians 12:21). The holy man is exalted when he sees those being helped by him becoming better. And a father, having rejoiced over children and being glad, is exalted. If I had been preserving the love which I was preserving toward them, toward me, I would not have been humbled, but I would have been exalted, having such as equals, having sharers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul's third visit takes the place of the witnesses by whom every word is established.
comments.comment: behold, this third time I come to you, so that having the third visit instead of three witnesses, we may be certain. … For if by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word is brought forth according to a judgment, it is established and confirmed; thus it was necessary through the two appearances of which I have made you certain. And since you need the fullness of being confirmed, I decided to answer you a third time.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Paul speaks of coming a third time and of two or three witnesses.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul warns those who had sinned that he will not spare them, and he promises that Christ, who is powerful among them and speaks in him, will carry out his rebuke.
comments.comment: He threatens those in Corinth who had sinned before (2 Corinthians 12:21) that, if they would not do what was fitting and live in holiness, he would not spare them again (2 Corinthians 13:2). The word “again” recalls the indignation he had already shown. And he tries to persuade them further that, should he rebuke those who stumble, his word will surely take effect, arguing as it were from what has already passed and from what is expected to come. This is why he says: “If you seek proof of Christ speaking in me” (2 Corinthians 13:3). For it is likely, he says, that you are waiting to see, the second time as well, whether Christ really speaks in me and carries His rebukes through to the end. Do not think, he says, as some who are still unbelieving and insolent think, that He is weak; for He is powerful among you (2 Corinthians 13:3), clearly among those who have believed and have come under Him, to whom He grants the care they need, and whom He turns back when they go wrong. So He is powerful among you; for He acts as God and shows the words of the saints to be true. And you will find my word strong in every way and at every point; for it is not I myself who speak, but rather Christ who is in me (Matthew 10:20).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul threatens and why he says Christ speaks in him.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Paul answers those scandalized by the cross: test who speaks in him by your own case, for Christ was not weak toward you but showed you strong through his Spirit.
comments.comment: “Since you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me, who toward you is not weak but is powerful in you. For he was also crucified from weakness, but he lives from God’s power.” (2 Corinthians 13:3–4) Some of those who had believed in our Lord Jesus Christ were scandalized, perhaps carried by words from certain people toward thoughts like these: If he was truly God and Son by nature of the God who is able in all things, how did he not escape the killers’ plots? And how, having endured the most dishonorable death on wood, would he not reasonably be thought to have been weak as we are? Toward such things the inspired Paul says: For if you should wish to test rightly who and how great is the one who speaks in me, having considered your own case you will find a sufficient grasp. For he was not weak in you, but rather showed you most powerful through his own Spirit.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On the True Faith, to the Empresses Pulcheria and Eudocia

comments.capsule: Christ was crucified in weakness as a man, but he rose by a power that is divine and beyond words.
comments.comment: But since he mentions those who, out of utter folly, supposed that Christ was truly weak because He endured the cross and bore the perversity, or rather the impiety, of the Jews, he makes a useful defence. He brings the power of the mystery forward at the right moment, and explains the willing self-emptying of the Only-begotten (Philippians 2:7) and the incomparable pre-eminence of the glory that came after it. “Yes,” he says, “He was crucified out of weakness” (2 Corinthians 13:4), as at least those still far from believing suppose among themselves; He suffered as man, and willingly endured death in the flesh. But they needed to know this as well: that having despoiled Hades and trampled the might of death, He came back to life on the third day, using not human power but power divine and beyond words.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ willingly took weakness in the flesh, yet he lives by a power that is his own, and the power of God is the Son himself.
comments.comment:
For it befits God alone to be able to do all things, so as even to destroy the power of death itself, and to crown the body held fast by corruption with the grace of incorruption. So He willingly endured being weak for a little while, as far as the nature of the flesh is concerned, just as He is indeed said to have hungered (Matthew 4:2), to have thirsted (John 19:28), and to have grown weary (John 4:6), and even to have died, for the sake of the economy.

Yet He lives by the power of God (2 Corinthians 13:4). He did not receive the power to do all things from another, but has it of Himself and possesses it in His very being; for the One who suffered in the flesh for us is God by nature. So if they stumble over the cross, let them marvel at the resurrection. And even if He is said to live by the power of God, you will none the less understand the power of God to be the Son Himself (1 Corinthians 1:24).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Christ could be both crucified in weakness and alive by God's power.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ was crucified not from weakness of his own but from what he took on himself for us.
comments.comment: Just as Christ was said to have become sin and a curse, being neither sin nor a curse, but he took upon himself our evils so that we might be delivered from them; so also now, he is said to have been crucified not from his own weakness, but from that which he received on our behalf, the dispensations on our behalf.
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala

comments.capsule: In the cross Christ underwent human weakness, but by the power of God he lives, and Christ himself is God's power.
comments.comment: He says therefore: 'he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God' (2 Corinthians 13:4). As far as it reached human weakness, he underwent the cross. Therefore this God was not able to undergo it, but man was able to suffer this. And indeed he has suffered, but by the power of God he lives. The power, therefore, of God is Christ, as he is God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Paul's authority is given to build up, not to destroy.
comments.comment: I had authority over you to build you up as a city and a temple of God; and this authority I want to bear fruit, through which I write teaching that I have authority not for destruction, but for building up.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what Paul's authority is for.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: After his exhortation Paul advises oneness of mind, so that peace and the love of God may dwell among them.
comments.comment: After all exhortation, he advises, having taken up oneness of mind, to hasten toward a good end; possessing themselves, they will receive genuine virtue and faith. For thus they have support, thinking the same thing, bringing peace, so that the space of the love of God might come to be among them. For this presence will make it an immovable possession for them, as each one imitating the teacher, to say: who will separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus? And the following.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Paul's closing exhortation to agreement is meant to bring.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The blessing brings the grace of Jesus, the love of God and the communion of the Spirit, who makes holy those who share in it.
comments.comment: It shall be, he says, for those thus blessed, the grace of the Lord Jesus, that is, saving them without works or making them having been graced. And the love of God shall be with them according to which he loves them or they love him with all heart and soul, and the communion of the Holy Spirit approaches, making spiritual and holy those who partake of it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the closing blessing gives to those who receive it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind
